title: A union  in a tool's inputSchema crashes the turn with -32603
description:
`coerce_arguments` crashes with `TypeError: cannot use 'list' as a set element` when a tool declares a JSON Schema union type -- `"type": ["string", "number"]`, which the spec allows.

REPRO (no server needed):

    from python_acp.commands import parse_command, coerce_arguments
    c = parse_command('/zoo/zoo-types --either 7')
    coerce_arguments(c, {'type': 'object',
                         'properties': {'either': {'type': ['string', 'number']}}})
    # TypeError: cannot use 'list' as a set element (unhashable type: 'list')

On the wire, over stdio against the schema zoo:

    /zoo/zoo-types --a_string hi --either 7
    -> {"error": {"code": -32603, "message": "Internal error",
                  "data": {"reason": "cannot use 'list' as a set element ..."}}}

CAUSE: `_scalar` (commands.py:709) reads `declared = spec.get('type')` and then tests
`declared in {'number', 'integer'}` and `declared in {'object', 'array'}`. `x in <set>`
hashes x, so an unhashable `declared` raises rather than missing. `_coerce` (:691) is
safe because it uses `==`; `tool_command_hint` (:935) is safe because it guards with
`isinstance(declared, str)`. The set membership tests are the only unguarded readers.

Note the whole *turn* dies, not the one call: the TypeError escapes to the SDK and
`session/prompt` answers -32603. Every other bad-argument case in this file is a
`CommandError` the user can read and retry.

FOUND BY: the schema zoo (`pyacp-6kz`) added `zoo-types.either` as `['string','number']`
precisely because 'JSON Schema allows it and most form builders do not expect it'. It
turns out this agent did not expect it either. Nothing exercised it -- the zoo's tools
were never *called* in a test, only listed for their `_meta`.

FIX: guard the two membership tests on `isinstance(declared, str)`, or normalise a list
`type` to None (no declared type -> `_maybe_json`, which is the honest reading: a union
says the tool accepts more than one type, so guessing from the text is exactly right).
Prefer the latter -- it makes `--either 7` arrive as `7` and `--either seven` as
`\"seven\"`, both legal under the union.

ACCEPTANCE: a union `type` coerces without raising and without a schema-driven refusal;
a test calls every schema-zoo tool through a real turn, not just lists it; the -32603
path is gone. `make lint && make docs-check && make test` pass.
close_reason: Closed

title: [bug] Every MCP tool is advertised as a command the parser then refuses
description:
`_commands_for` (turn_mcp_router.py:1579) announces every MCP tool as an
`AvailableCommand` named `<server>/<tool>`, and `parse_command` (commands.py) recognises
only the seven built-in names. So the agent advertises commands it cannot accept.

Observed live in acp-ui. The session announced eight commands:

    Demo/echo      Echoes text            <- from tools/list
    tools, invokeTool, listPrompts, promptShow, promptInvoke, listResources, resourceShow

The user typed the first one and got:

    /Demo/echo foo bar
    -> Prompt block 0 is not JSON (Expecting value). Each text block must be ...

`parse_command("/Demo/echo --text foo")` returns `None`, so `_command_in` falls through to
the JSON convention and the prompt is refused as malformed JSON. The message is about the
JSON convention, which the user was not using and had no reason to think they were.

This is precisely the failure the `acp-protocol` skill's central rule exists to prevent --
"an advertisement is a promise, and a promise is testable". `available_commands` is what a
client fills its composer from; commands.md even says so ("A client that fills its composer
from `available_commands` sends the name it was given"). Nothing tests that the names it
sends are names `parse_command` accepts, and **no test anywhere types an advertised tool
command** -- grep for `Demo/echo` or `_commands_for` in tests/ returns nothing.

Second half of the same defect: the per-tool `AvailableCommand` carries **no `input`
hint**, while every built-in does. So even a client that could send the name gives the
user nothing about how to pass arguments -- the observed `/Demo/echo foo bar` is someone
guessing positionally because nothing said `--text`.
close_reason: Closed

title: [bug] Agent message text is preformatted plain text, but clients render it as markdown
description:
Everything we emit in an ACP `agent_message_chunk` is column-aligned plain text
containing `<angle>` placeholders. Real ACP clients render that field as
**markdown**, so the text arrives mangled.

Found while debugging a live acp-ui (formulahendry/acp-ui v0.1.16) session against
`--transport stdio`. `ChatView.vue:228` is `v-html="marked.parse(content)"`; Zed
renders agent messages as markdown too, so this is the norm, not one client's quirk.

Two independent failures, both visible in one message:

1. **Placeholders vanish.** `<name>`, `<string>`, `<integer>`, `<any>`, `<value>`,
   `<server>`, `<tool>` parse as HTML tags and are dropped by the browser. The
   observed refusal read:
       {"tool": "", "arguments": {...}, "server": ""}
   where the wire carried `"<name>"` in both slots.

2. **Column alignment is destroyed.** `_INDENT` is two spaces (commands.py:589), so a
   4-space-indented parameter line follows a 2-space-indented tool name with no blank
   line between them. CommonMark forbids an indented code block from interrupting a
   paragraph, so it is a lazy continuation instead: marked collapses the whole listing
   into one run-on line.

`render_tool_listing` for one server with one tool renders as:

    1 tool on 1 server.

    mock (1 tool)

      mock/echo
        --text  <string>    required  What to echo
        --times <integer>

    Call one with:
      /invokeTool mock/echo --text <value>

and reaches the user as `mock/echo --text required What to echo --times` followed by
`Call one with: /invokeTool mock/echo --text`.

Tests never caught it because they assert against the raw string
(tests/test_commands.py:219 and friends), which is exactly the text that is correct
on the wire and wrong on screen.
acceptance_criteria:
Preformatted blocks (tool/prompt/resource listings, prompt+resource headings) are emitted inside fenced code blocks; inline placeholders in prose are wrapped in code spans.
Rendering `render_tool_listing`, `render_prompt_listing`, `render_resource_listing`, `render_prompt_heading`, `render_resource_contents`, `_example`, `_no_servers`, the `commands.py:368` parse error, and `turn_mcp_router.CONVENTION` through a CommonMark parser preserves every `<...>` placeholder and every column.
AvailableCommand `input.hint` and `description` are UNCHANGED — CommandPalette.vue interpolates them with `{{ }}`, which escapes HTML, so backticks there would render literally.
A test asserts the markdown-safety property itself, not just the literal strings.
tests/transcripts/*.json regenerated via `make transcripts` with the diff read.
make lint && make docs-check && make test pass.
close_reason: Closed

title: The command announcement loses a race with a pipelined session/prompt
description:
tests/test_interop.py::test_a_foreign_client_runs_a_tool_and_sees_the_whole_update_stream
failed on Python 3.11 and passed on 3.12/3.13/3.14. Reproduced locally: 4 runs in 5 on
3.11, 0 in 8 on 3.14. The palette arrived one place late --
["user_message_chunk", "available_commands_update", ...] instead of
["available_commands_update", "user_message_chunk", ...].

NOT a version-specific behaviour difference. It is a genuine sub-millisecond race that
3.14 happens to win and 3.11 mostly loses, and it was on the WIRE, not in the client's
dispatch -- confirmed with a stream observer on the interop client, which records
arrival order in the receive loop.

CAUSE. announcer.py's stream observer fires after the session/new response bytes are
written, which is correct and necessary. But an observer is a TASK, and it called
agent.announce_commands, which builds the list first -- a tools/list round trip per
backend. Awaiting that parks the observer on real subprocess I/O. The SDK's own client
pipelines: it sends session/prompt the instant new_session returns. That request gets
read and its turn's first session/update written while the observer is still waiting on
the MCP server, so user_message_chunk beats the palette onto the wire.

FIX. Build the list before the response, send it after. session/new and session/fork call
agent._prepare_commands, which stashes the list against the new id; the observer is wired
to a new announce_prepared_commands whose FIRST AWAIT IS THE SEND. That makes the
ordering a consequence of scheduling rather than a race:

  - acp.task.MessageSender is an ordered asyncio.Queue behind the stdio transport, and
    Queue.put on an unbounded queue does not suspend, so wire order is enqueue order.
  - The observer's task is created in _run_request's continuation, which is on the ready
    queue before the loop next polls for I/O -- so it is created ahead of any task the
    pipelined request could create.

The stash is one-shot and private to that door. announce_commands never reads it, so
every re-announcement (a catalogue server toggled on, a turn refreshing the palette)
rebuilds; a stash the general door could consume would pin the palette to whatever the
session started with. When nothing was prepared -- no executor listing, or a tools/list
that failed -- announce_prepared_commands falls back to building, trading the ordering
guarantee rather than the palette.

ALSO CORRECTED. announcer.py, announcer.md and agent.md all said "the SDK has no ordered
outgoing queue -- every sender awaits the transport directly". That is not true of
agent-client-protocol 0.12.1, which routes stdio sends through acp.task.MessageSender.
The conclusion it supported (a create_task from inside the handler still races the reply,
because it can reach the transport before the response is enqueued at all) survives, but
the stated reason was wrong and it is the crux of the new reasoning.
close_reason: Fixed: session/new and session/fork now call agent._prepare_commands, and the announcer observer is wired to announce_prepared_commands, whose first await is the send. tests/test_interop.py 10/10 on 3.11 (was 1/5). make lint + docs-check + test green on 3.11 and 3.14 (1156 passed). Also corrected the 'the SDK has no ordered outgoing queue' claim in announcer.py, announcer.md and agent.md -- acp.task.MessageSender is one.

title: Toggle a catalogue server mid-session, and re-announce the palette
description:
session/set_config_option on an 'mcp/<name>' id stops being a stored flag and becomes an action: turning it on spawns that server for the session, turning it off tears it down. Then the palette is re-announced, so what the client can call follows what it selected -- which is what pyacp-p8v built the announcement for.

McpBackendRegistry needs two methods it does not have. open() is all-or-nothing for a whole session and refuses a session that already has backends; this needs add(session_id, spec, elicit) and remove(session_id, name), both keeping _specs in step so a later fork inherits the session's ACTUAL selection rather than what it was created with. Roots are already stored per session, so add() reuses them rather than taking them again.

A TURN IN FLIGHT is the case to get right. Closing a backend while a tool call is running on it turns a live call into a broken pipe, and the client would see a backend error for something it did on purpose. session.turn_is_running already exists; a toggle while a turn is running is refused with a clear message rather than raced. Refusing is the honest answer: the client can cancel or wait, and neither silently loses work.

A spawn that FAILS on toggle-on must leave the option OFF and the session otherwise untouched -- the same all-or-nothing rule open() already keeps, at one server's granularity. It is an error to the client, not a killed session: the session was working a moment ago and still is.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Toggling on spawns the server; a following turn can call its tools.
2. Toggling off tears the subprocess down -- asserted by the conftest leak guard, not just by absence from the palette.
3. Either direction emits config_option_update and then available_commands_update.
4. A toggle while a turn is running is refused, and the session's servers are unchanged.
5. A failed spawn leaves the option false, the session alive, and no orphan process.
6. A fork after a toggle inherits the toggled selection, not the original.
7. Toggling a non-mcp option (announce-tools) still behaves exactly as before.
8. make lint && make docs-check && make test.
close_reason: Live toggle shipped: McpBackendRegistry.add/remove, agent refuses during a turn, reverts a failed spawn, re-announces options then palette. Epic complete — catalogue configured, advertised, selected, and switchable. 1151 tests pass.

title: Advertise the catalogue and open what a session selected
description:
Wire the catalogue in: --mcp-config on the CLI, the executor advertising one boolean per entry, and session/new and session/fork opening the entries a session has on -- alongside, not instead of, the servers a client named itself.

--mcp-config PATH on both transports. cli.py's _run docstring currently says 'No process-wide MCP server is started, and there is no flag to ask for one'; it has to say what is still true (no shared server, no passthrough, every subprocess still per-session) and what changed (there are now operator-supplied RECIPES a client may select).

session_config_options is a static class attribute on McpToolRouterExecutor today. It becomes an instance attribute: SESSION_CONFIG_OPTIONS + catalogue.config_options(). agent._config_options() already deep-copies per session, so a toggle on one session cannot move another.

NAME COLLISION between a catalogue entry and a client-supplied server is -32602 naming both. McpBackendRegistry.open already refuses duplicates with a ValueError, but that message says 'in session/new', which would be wrong and confusing when one of the two came from a config file.
acceptance_criteria:
1. --mcp-config on both transports; a bad path fails at startup, not at the first session.
2. A session with no catalogue behaves exactly as today -- this is the regression that matters.
3. session/new opens the enabled catalogue entries plus the client's own.
4. An entry with enabled=false is advertised but not opened.
5. A catalogue/client name collision is -32602 naming both sources.
6. session/fork with mcpServers omitted inherits the parent's actual selection.
7. The palette from pyacp-p8v carries the catalogue servers' tools.
8. make lint && make docs-check && make test.
close_reason: --mcp-config on both transports; catalogue advertised as config options and opened alongside client-supplied servers; collision refused; fork inherits selection. 1133 tests pass.

title: mcp_catalogue.py: the catalogue file and what it produces
description:
A new module that turns an operator's config file into two things: McpServerStdio specs to open, and SessionConfigOptionBoolean options to advertise. Nothing else -- no registry, no agent, no CLI.

FORMAT. TOML primary: tomllib is stdlib on 3.11, and a catalogue an operator maintains needs comments, which JSON cannot carry. JSON is ALSO accepted, dispatched on suffix, because {'mcpServers': {...}} is the de-facto shape every editor and desktop app already uses and an operator should be able to paste theirs. A bare top-level map is accepted in JSON too.

  [servers.tools]
  command = 'python'
  args = ['server.py']
  env = { LOG = 'debug' }
  description = 'Local demo tools'   # shown in the config option
  enabled = true                     # whether a NEW session starts with it on

ENV is a map in the file and becomes the list of EnvVariable the SDK wants -- env is not optional on the wire, an entry that omits it is dropped (pyacp-mej).

VALIDATION is the point of the module. A catalogue that half-parses is worse than one that fails: name must be non-empty and contain no '/', since '<server>/<tool>' is how a tool call is routed and how the palette carries server identity; command must be a non-empty string; args and env values must be strings; an unknown key is an error, not a shrug, because a typo'd 'commmand' would otherwise produce a server that never starts.
acceptance_criteria:
1. load(path) returns an ordered catalogue; order is the file's, not sorted, so an operator controls what a settings panel shows first.
2. TOML and JSON both parse to the same catalogue for equivalent content.
3. specs() returns McpServerStdio with env as EnvVariable entries.
4. config_options() returns one SessionConfigOptionBoolean per entry, id 'mcp/<name>', currentValue from 'enabled'.
5. Every validation failure names the file, the entry, and what was wrong.
6. A name containing '/' is refused.
7. A missing file is a clear error, not a traceback.
8. Sibling mcp_catalogue.md; make lint && make docs-check && make test.
close_reason: mcp_catalogue.py + .md + 29 tests. TOML and JSON, namespaced config ids, loud validation.

title: Agent-side MCP catalogue a client selects from
description:
Today the only way a session gets MCP servers is a client naming command lines in session/new. That is correct for ACP's canonical topology -- an editor SPAWNS the agent over stdio, so it is the parent handing its own config to a child. On the WebSocket bridge the topology inverts: python-acp is a long-lived server an operator configures, clients connect later, and requiring each of them to know a server's argv is backwards. It is also arbitrary process execution by request: any client past the access key can make this process spawn any binary.

So the agent gets a CATALOGUE of MCP servers, configured by the operator, and the client SELECTS from it. Native ACP, no extension: one SessionConfigOptionBoolean per catalogue entry, advertised in NewSessionResponse.configOptions, toggled with session/set_config_option, re-announced as config_option_update -- a multi-select in all but name, since ACP's select variant is single-choice.

NOT A REVERSAL OF pyacp-sld.4. What that removed was --mcp-command: ONE process-wide server shared by every client, plus a passthrough letting a client drive it directly. A catalogue is a set of RECIPES. Sessions stay isolated, each still spawns its own subprocesses, each still dies with its session. Say this in cli.py's _run docstring, which currently reads 'no process-wide MCP server is started, and there is no flag to ask for one'.

DECIDED WITH THE USER 2026-08-27:
1. Catalogue comes from a config file (--mcp-config).
2. A client may toggle servers ANY TIME mid-session, not only at session/new.
3. session/new's client-supplied mcpServers STAYS, alongside the catalogue.
design:
Three pieces, in order:

1. mcp_catalogue.py -- parse the file into ordered entries; produce McpServerStdio specs and SessionConfigOptionBoolean options. Pure; no registry, no agent.
2. Selection at session open -- the CLI flag, the executor advertising the options, session/new and session/fork opening the enabled entries alongside client-supplied servers.
3. Live toggle -- set_config_option on an mcp/* id opens or closes that one backend and re-announces the palette.

Config option ids are NAMESPACED 'mcp/<name>' so a catalogue entry cannot collide with announce-tools or on-tool-failure.

The palette is the reason this lands well now: pyacp-p8v made session/new announce available_commands, so toggling a server can re-announce and the client's palette follows.
close_reason: Live toggle shipped: McpBackendRegistry.add/remove, agent refuses during a turn, reverts a failed spawn, re-announces options then palette. Epic complete — catalogue configured, advertised, selected, and switchable. 1151 tests pass.

title: __version__ is a second version literal, and nothing binds it to pyproject
description:
src/python_acp/__init__.py carries __version__ = '0.1.0' while pyproject.toml says 0.2.0. agent.py reports __version__ as initialize's agentInfo.version, so the wheel and the wire disagree about what this agent is. Found while checking release readiness for v0.2.0; tagging as-is ships a 0.2.0 wheel that identifies itself as 0.1.0 to every client.

The three existing tests (test_agent, test_transport_ws, test_transport_stdio) all assert the wire equals __version__, comparing the constant to itself, so 898 green tests said nothing about this.
acceptance_criteria: __version__ matches the installed distribution metadata, and a test fails when they drift
close_reason: Closed

title: WebSocket transport accepts any client that can open the socket
description:
serve() is called with no process_request hook, no Origin check, and no TLS, and AUTH_METHODS is empty by decision, so nothing authenticates a WebSocket client. session/new spawns an arbitrary command, so an unauthenticated socket on a non-loopback interface is remote code execution as whoever runs the bridge. The default bind of 127.0.0.1 is the only thing containing it, and README's container recipe tells the reader to pass --host 0.0.0.0 with -p 8765:8765, which publishes it on every host interface without saying what that exposes.

Scope: a pre-handshake access key. The server reads PYTHON_ACP_WS_KEY from the environment; a client presents it as a ?key= query parameter on the WebSocket URL; process_request rejects a mismatch with 401 before the handshake. Binding a non-loopback host with no key refuses to start unless PYTHON_ACP_WS_ALLOW_UNAUTHENTICATED=1 is set. Loopback with no key is unchanged.

This is transport admission control, below ACP. It does not touch AUTH_METHODS or the capability manifest: an unauthorized client never gets to send initialize.
design: Env var rather than a CLI flag, because argv is world-readable via ps and a secret does not belong there. secrets.compare_digest for the comparison. The refuse-to-start guard lives in the transport rather than cli.py so a library embedder gets it too.
acceptance_criteria: A key set and matched connects; mismatched or absent gets 401 before the handshake; non-loopback bind with no key exits non-zero naming the env var; the opt-out env var overrides it; loopback with no key behaves as before; README documents the key and the container recipe uses it; make lint docs-check test green
close_reason: Closed

title: Interop smoke test against a real ACP client over stdio
description:
The verification that cannot be faked by our own test suite: a client we did not write completes a session against python-acp over stdio.

Options are the SDK's own example clients under examples/, or a real editor integration (Zed, Neovim). Prefer something runnable in CI; if nothing is, make it a documented manual procedure with recorded output rather than skipping it.

This is the payoff for decision D2 -- it is the check that 'strict full ACP v1' means something outside this repository.
acceptance_criteria: A third-party ACP client completes initialize, session creation, a prompt turn with streamed updates, and clean shutdown against python-acp over stdio; the procedure is automated in CI or documented as a manual runbook with recorded output; failures are diagnosable from the captured transcript.
notes: pyacp-tzd.2 delivered the stdio binding and a subprocess-level test (tests/test_transport_stdio.py) that drives 'python -m python_acp.cli --transport stdio' with the SDK's own ClientSideConnection via acp.stdio.spawn_agent_process. That covers startup, JSON-RPC framing over a pipe, initialize, and clean exit - but the client is the SDK's, not a third party's, and no session is created because session/new is still -32601 until pyacp-3rw.2. This bead remains the real-client, full-session check.
close_reason: Two halves. AUTOMATED: tests/interop/acp_client.py runs as its own process importing only acp (asserted via AST), completing initialize/session-new-with-own-MCP-server/tool-running prompt/refused prompt/list/close/clean-exit over a pipe; tests/test_interop.py asserts the recorded transcript. RECORDED: the SDK's examples/client.py driven against us, transcript and upstream commit in docs/interop.md, with the honest note that it hardcodes mcp_servers=[] so it cannot reach a tool. FINDING: the SDK's reference client refuses session/request_permission, which pyacp-8bv.1 treated as a broken client and refused the turn for -- reproduced, corrected to proceed-and-announce, and scoped to this executor because an LLM-backed one would need the decision remade. 478 tests.

title: Build the method-by-method ACP conformance suite
description:
Test every method in Phase 0.2's compliance matrix against its disposition: implemented methods behave per spec, declined methods return the correct error. The matrix is the checklist; a method absent from the suite is a gap in the matrix or the suite.

Structure it so adding an Agent method without adding conformance coverage is visibly incomplete. This suite is what makes the Phase 7 removal safe, so it must be trustworthy before that lands.
acceptance_criteria: Every Agent method in the matrix has conformance coverage matching its disposition; declined methods are asserted to return the correct error, not merely to fail; the suite runs under make test on all four matrix Python versions; a new method with no coverage is detectable.
notes: pyacp-4ns.2: cases derive mechanically from docs/acp-compliance-matrix.md, including the declines. See its 'What Phase 8 tests' section - notably the both-directions test for the three unstable-gated methods, and pinning -32601 for session/delete, logout, providers/*, nes/*, and document/* so a future SDK bump that starts routing them is noticed.
close_reason: tests/test_conformance.py: 62 cases from one CONFORMANCE table covering all 15 Agent members. Declines assert the correct error (-32601 with data.method; -32000 for authenticate), unstable three tested both directions, 16 unrouted AGENT_METHODS names pinned as unregistered, and every advertised capability mapped to the method it promises and called. Gap detection verified by deleting a row (4 tests catch it). Cross-version bug found and fixed: Agent.__protocol_attrs__ is 3.12+ and empty on 3.11, so the member walk passed vacuously on the project floor; replaced with vars(Agent) and pinned. 470 tests pass on 3.11 and 3.14.

title: Call session/request_permission from the turn executor
description:
CORRECTION FROM THE ORIGINAL PLAN: request_permission is an acp.interfaces.Client method. The agent CALLS it; it does not implement it. The original plan's 'Implement session/request_permission' was backwards.

Before a consequential tool call, ask the client for permission with the tool call and the available PermissionOptions, and honor the answer. Handle the cancellation outcome -- the client can cancel the turn while the permission prompt is open, which must land as stopReason cancelled (Phase 3.5), not as a denied permission.

Evaluate acp.contrib.permissions, which ships a permission broker.
acceptance_criteria: The executor requests permission before consequential tool calls and honors allow, deny, and always-variants; cancellation while a prompt is open produces stopReason cancelled; behavior when the client does not support permissions is defined and tested; which tool calls are consequential is documented; whether acp.contrib.permissions is used is recorded with a reason.
notes:
pyacp-hnk.1: session/request_permission has NO capability gate -- ClientCapabilities has no field for it and every ACP client must accept it. Do not add one to turns.Gate. Call it straight off context.client.
CORRECTED by pyacp-6ni.4. This bead decided a client answering -32601 to
session/request_permission was broken and refused the turn. The SDK's own
examples/client.py answers exactly that, and the interop run reproduced the failure: a
well-formed tool invocation came back stopReason refusal with the tool never run.

New behaviour: the turn PROCEEDS and announces it once per session via an
agent_message_chunk. The client named the tool and arguments in session/prompt itself, so
the authorization already exists -- the prompt was a courtesy to a human who might be
watching, and a client that cannot reach one has already decided.

SCOPE: this reasoning is specific to the deterministic tool router. An LLM-backed executor
CHOOSES the tool, so a client's prompt authorizes nothing in particular and the same
fallback would be a hole. Any executor added later must decide it again. Stated at the
fallback in turn_mcp_router.py and in docs/interop.md.
close_reason: The router calls session/request_permission before every tool call (all calls are consequential: MCP 2024-11-05 has no tool annotations, follow-up filed). Denial vs cancellation kept distinct -- DeniedOutcome's literal is 'cancelled', so a reject option marks the call failed and continues while a cancelled outcome returns stopReason cancelled without raising CancelledError (agent.prompt reads turn.cancelled(), and a raised CancelledError would leave the request unanswered). always-variants remembered on the Session, copied by fork. A client refusing the mandatory method gets a refusal. acp.contrib.permissions.PermissionBroker USED; its default option set is missing reject_always so we add the fourth. 407 tests; verified against a real ACP client over stdio.

title: Get stopReason semantics right, especially cancelled
description:
prompt must return the correct stopReason for every exit path: normal completion, cancellation, refusal, and any limit condition the executor can hit.

'cancelled' is called out in the plan's verification because it is the one most easily got wrong -- a cancelled turn must return the response with stopReason cancelled, not raise, not hang, and not return end_turn. It also has to interleave correctly with in-flight session/update notifications and with an MCP call still running in the backend.

Pairs with Phase 1.5's $/cancel_request registry; these are two different cancellation mechanisms and both must be verified.
acceptance_criteria: Each exit path returns its correct stopReason; cancelling mid-turn returns stopReason cancelled promptly rather than raising or hanging; no session/update notifications are emitted after the turn response; an in-flight MCP call is cancelled or abandoned cleanly; tests cover cancel-before-start, cancel-mid-tool-call, and cancel-after-completion.
notes:
pyacp-hnk.1 completed the seam in src/python_acp/turns.py. What is now there:
- TurnExecutor: async execute(context, prompt) -> TurnResult. Single method, async, no
  step count and no rule against client round-trips mid-turn, so multi-step/interactive
  turns are open by construction (held by test_a_turn_may_be_multi_step_and_interactive).
- TurnResult(stop_reason, usage=None), TurnResult.ended(). agent.prompt fills
  PromptResponse.usage from it. The type can already express all five stopReasons.
- TurnContext: session, client, session_id, emit(update), gates, allows(gate),

title: Define the TurnExecutor interface
description:
Decision D3's seam. Define the interface a prompt turn runs behind: it receives the session and its content blocks, may call client methods (Phase 4), emits session/update notifications, and returns a stopReason.

This is what makes 'no LLM in the loop' a design choice rather than a dead end, and it satisfies the original Phase 6.3 'backend abstraction for non-MCP executors' in the same stroke.

Design it so an LLM-backed executor is droppable in later without reopening the interface -- specifically, do not assume the turn is synchronous, single-step, or free of client round-trips.
acceptance_criteria: A documented TurnExecutor interface with streaming update emission, client-method access, cancellation, and stopReason return; the deterministic executor and at least one test double both implement it; the interface does not assume a single-step or non-interactive turn; sibling .md written; the seam is reflected in ARCHITECTURE.md.
notes:
pyacp-3rw.2 seeded src/python_acp/turns.py because this bead depends on it and
session/prompt had to be wired to something; putting a provisional seam in agent.py would
have violated module-boundaries (agent.py is method-shaped translation only). Recorded as
decision B6b.

What is there: TurnExecutor Protocol with one `async execute(context, prompt) -> StopReason`;
TurnContext(session, client) exposing session_id and `emit(update)` (which supplies the
session id itself so an executor cannot address another session); IdleTurnExecutor, the
default that completes a turn having done nothing and logs a warning.

Because the call is async and single-method, nothing assumes the turn is synchronous,
single-step, or free of client round-trips -- this bead's stated constraint.

What this bead must STILL add (also listed in src/python_acp/turns.md):
- stopReason beyond end_turn/cancelled: max_tokens, max_turn_requests, refusal (hnk.5)
- capability-gated client-method access; context.client is the raw facade today
- a cancellation token, so an executor can run async cleanup without racing the cancel
- content-block typing; `prompt` is list[Any] and the promptCapabilities literals stay
  false in AGENT_CAPABILITY_MANIFEST until hnk.3 enforces them
- a TurnResult carrying usage; PromptResponse.usage exists and nothing fills it

agent.py already owns the cancelled path: the turn runs as its own task and
asyncio.wait({turn}) + turn.cancelled() distinguishes "session/cancel reached it" from
"this request was cancelled". Do not change that to `await turn` -- it makes the two
indistinguishable.

title: Add a request registry and cooperative cancellation for $/cancel_request
description:
There is no cancellation anywhere in the runtime today. Add a per-connection registry of in-flight requests and cooperative cancellation driven by $/cancel_request, so a client can abandon work rather than wait out a timeout.

Distinct from session/cancel (Phase 3.5), which cancels a prompt turn and must produce stopReason 'cancelled'. This one cancels an individual JSON-RPC request. Both must work; they are different mechanisms and the plan's verification calls for both to be tested.

Interacts with pyacp-ua1: when a cancelled request has an MCP call in flight, the backend should be told via notifications/cancelled rather than left computing a reply nobody reads.
acceptance_criteria: In-flight requests are tracked per connection and cancellable by id; $/cancel_request cancels cooperatively without killing the connection or sibling requests; a cancelled request produces the correct ACP error; cancellation propagates to an in-flight MCP call; tests cover cancelling mid-flight, cancelling an unknown id, and cancelling an already-completed request.

pyacp-4ns.3 finding: grep of SDK 0.12.1 meta.py, connection.py, and router.py turns up no route or constant for $/cancel_request anywhere. AGENT_METHODS carries session/cancel only. pyacp-4ns.2 re-confirmed against the installed 0.12.1: no $/cancel_request route exists in acp/meta.py, acp/router.py, or acp/agent/router.py. ACP cancellation is the session/cancel notification (CancelNotification -> Agent.cancel), which pyacp-3rw.2 and pyacp-hnk.5 already cover. Either this bead means the JSON-RPC-level cancel and must build it on ext_method, or it is a misreading of the spec and should be closed against session/cancel. Decide before implementing.

pyacp-tzd.6 finding, for the "$/cancel_request has no home" question: acp.schema.Error accepts -32800 in its code literal union, alongside the six JSON-RPC standard codes and ACP's -32000/-32002. acp.RequestError supplies NO constructor for it and the schema carries no description; it appears nowhere else in the SDK. -32800 is LSP's RequestCancelled, which ACP's error shape otherwise mirrors. Could not confirm against upstream ACP docs (schema/rust sources 404 at the URLs tried). errors.py now exposes REQUEST_CANCELLED = -32800 and request_cancelled(reason=None) on that reading, with the uncertainty documented in errors.md; confirm before putting it on the wire. Also settled by tzd.6: asyncio.CancelledError is never mapped to a RequestError -- to_request_error re-raises it, because returning a value from a cancelled coroutine tells asyncio the cancellation did not take. Whatever reports a cancellation must do so after letting the exception propagate.

Verified against upstream agentclientprotocol/agent-client-protocol main (agent-client-protocol-schema/src/v1/agent.rs, client.rs, rpc.rs, ext.rs): the only cancellation in the protocol is the session/cancel notification (SESSION_CANCEL_METHOD_NAME). The SDK 0.12.1 CancelRequestNotification model at acp/schema.py:2636 is an orphan -- no AGENT_METHODS/CLIENT_METHODS entry, not in the ClientNotification params union, referenced nowhere in the SDK, and no wire name exists for it anywhere. description:

title: A schema zoo in the mock MCP server, for testing ACP clients against every JSON Schema construct
description:
pyacp-ma2 makes python-acp publish each MCP tool's inputSchema on
AvailableCommand._meta, so a client can render a real form. Nothing in this repo
exercises that with a schema worth rendering: the fixture's echo declares one required
string, and every other tool declares properties: {}. A client author wiring up a form has
nothing to point at, and neither do we when a rendering bug is reported.

Add an opt-in family of tools to tests/fixtures/mock_mcp_server.py -- MOCK_MCP_SCHEMA_ZOO=1
-- covering every construct on both sides of the line acp-ui draws:

RENDERED, so a client can see each widget in isolation:
  every JSON type bare (string, number, integer, boolean, array, object, null)
  string constraints: minLength, maxLength, pattern, and the formats (email, date,
    date-time, uri, uuid)
  numeric constraints: minimum, maximum, exclusiveMinimum, exclusiveMaximum, multipleOf,
    and integer against number
  the three ways to spell a choice: bare enum, enum + enumNames, and oneOf with const and
    title -- these render as three different dropdowns and a client gets them wrong
    independently
  arrays: of scalars, of enums, of objects, with minItems / maxItems
  required against optional against defaulted, and dependentRequired
  nested objects

DECLINED, so the fallback path is testable too: if/then/else, dependentSchemas, allOf, and
discriminated oneOf, each as its own tool. acp-ui steps aside to a plain text box with a
reason for these; a client that instead renders a subset of a conditional schema shows the
user a form that is confidently wrong, which is worse than the text box.

EDGES, which are the ones our own code already claims to handle:
  properties: {} -- a statement that the tool takes no parameters
  NO inputSchema at all -- said nothing. This is the case _tool_meta omits the key for,
    and today it can only be unit-tested because the fixture cannot produce it. This tool
    makes that branch reachable over the wire.

tools/call on any zoo tool echoes the arguments back as JSON. That is the round trip that
matters: it shows what JSON types the client's form and this bridge's coerce_arguments
actually produced, so `--count 3` arriving as 3 rather than "3" is visible rather than
assumed.

Usable outside the suite, which is the point: `make run` already prints the demo server
command for pasting into session/new, and McpServerStdio carries env, so a client author
adds MOCK_MCP_SCHEMA_ZOO=1 there and gets the whole zoo in their palette.
design:
Opt-in, exactly like MOCK_MCP_ANNOTATED_TOOLS. Every unrelated test in the suite expects this server to offer one tool, and the annotated-tools knob exists because that was already learned once.

One tool per concern rather than one kitchen-sink tool. A single tool carrying every construct renders as one enormous form, and when it renders wrong nothing says which construct broke. Separate tools also mean the four declined constructs get four separate fallbacks to look at instead of one.

The no-inputSchema tool is deliberately off-spec -- MCP's Tool declares inputSchema required -- and the comment must say so. It is there because servers in the wild omit it and commands.py already distinguishes that case from properties: {} in its error messages; a fixture that cannot produce it leaves our handling of it untested against a real server.

Add a test asserting the zoo is off by default, and one asserting the schemas reach _meta intact over the wire -- that is the pyacp-ma2 verbatim-pass-through claim, checked against a server rather than a dict.
acceptance_criteria: MOCK_MCP_SCHEMA_ZOO=1 adds tools covering the rendered constructs, the four declined ones, and both edges (empty properties, absent inputSchema); the zoo is absent by default and no existing test changes; tools/call echoes arguments back as JSON; a test proves a zoo schema arrives in AvailableCommand._meta unmodified; make lint && make docs-check && make test pass.
notes:
Prompted by acp-ui building the client half of pyacp-ma2 now. The rendered/declined split is
theirs, from docs/agent-integration.md, rendered at
https://claude.ai/code/artifact/c8a3af41-643c-4ccf-9f53-b643a35f2df7 -- treat their list as
the coverage target but not as a spec we own, since their rendering rules can change
without ours changing.

The precedent to copy is the every-content tool in the same fixture: one place where every
variant of a thing is served at once, including the deliberately broken ones, so a mapping
is exercised against a real server rather than a hand-built dict.

Related: pyacp-ma2 emits the schemas, pyacp-qvh documents the contract, pyacp-8lp pins the
rest of the acp-ui checklist.

--- IMPLEMENTED ---

MOCK_MCP_SCHEMA_ZOO=1 adds 13 tools to the first tools/list page. Verified end to end
through a real session; announced palette:

  zoo-types               9 props   every JSON type bare, plus an untyped property and a
                                    two-type union
  zoo-strings             8 props   minLength/maxLength/pattern, five formats, and one
                                    format nobody has heard of
  zoo-numbers             4 props   inclusive and exclusive bounds, multipleOf, unbounded
  zoo-choices             5 props   bare enum / enum+enumNames / oneOf+const, plus const
                                    and a non-string enum
  zoo-arrays              5 props   scalars, enums, objects, minItems/maxItems, no items
  zoo-required            5 props   required / optional / defaulted + dependentRequired
  zoo-nested              2 props   objects two deep
  zoo-if-then-else        2 props   declined by acp-ui
  zoo-dependent-schemas   2 props   declined
  zoo-all-of              0 props   declined
  zoo-one-of              0 props   declined
  zoo-empty               0 props   properties: {} -- "takes no parameters"
  zoo-silent              _meta inputSchema key OMITTED -- "said nothing"

Worth knowing: zoo-all-of and zoo-one-of announce a hint of "(no parameters)" because
their properties live inside the composition keyword, not at the top level, and
tool_command_hint can only walk what it can see. That is not a bug in either place -- it
is the argument for _meta in one line, since a client holding the schema sees two
parameters the hint could not mention. Commented as such in the fixture and in
turn_mcp_router.md so nobody "fixes" it.

For a client author: `make run` prints the demo server command; add

and oneOf/const survive, conditionals are forwarded whole), the two edges stay
distinguishable on the wire, and a zoo tool echoes back the JSON types coerce_arguments
produced.

title: Publish the tool-schema _meta contract so clients and MCP servers can rely on it
description:
pyacp-ma2 makes python-acp *emit* each MCP tool's inputSchema on
AvailableCommand._meta. That is half a contract. The other half is telling the two
populations on either side of this bridge that the channel exists, what is in it, and what
they get by filling it in well. Neither can discover it from our source, and _meta is by
definition a key nobody may assume anything about -- ACP says implementations MUST NOT
make assumptions about _meta values, which is exactly why an undocumented one is inert.

Two audiences, one document, because the two halves only make sense together: the schema a
server writes is the form a client renders, with python-acp as the pipe and no
intelligence of its own in between.

FOR ACP CLIENTS -- "here is a capability we offer you":

  The key: _meta["python-acp/tool"], carrying server, tool and inputSchema. Namespaced
  deliberately; state that a bare _meta.inputSchema fallback is a convention other agents
  may adopt without adopting our namespace, so this is an idea to copy rather than a
  python-acp feature.
  Verbatim pass-through: what we send is what tools/list returned, unnormalised and
  unreordered. A client is rendering the *server's* vocabulary, not ours. Say so, because
  it tells a client author that any weirdness in a schema is upstream of us and that
  cleaning it up on their side re-introduces the disagreement we avoided.
  Omitted, never null, when a tool publishes no schema -- and the difference is load-
  bearing: commands.md already distinguishes "properties: {} means takes no parameters"
  from "no inputSchema means nothing was said". A client should draw the same
  distinction.
  Degrade, never fail: a malformed or absent _meta must cost the user nothing but the
  form. The hint string is unchanged and always present.
  Validation is still ours: coerce_arguments (commands.py:638) remains the authority and a
  client-side form is a convenience, not a trust boundary. A client author should know we
  will re-check, so they need not fear being the last line of defence -- and so they do not
  build one.
  Where it is announced: both the per-turn available_commands_update and the
  once-per-session announcement, from the single _commands_for
  (turn_mcp_router.py:1589) -- plus whatever pyacp-ma2 concludes about the payload cost,
  since a client author needs to know if the two lists can differ.

FOR MCP SERVER AUTHORS -- "your inputSchema is now user-visible; write it with intention":

  This is the part nobody currently knows. A server author writes inputSchema believing it
  is machine-facing validation; through this bridge it becomes the form a human fills in.
  That changes what "good" means, and the specific fields that pay off should be named:
  title and description become labels and help text; enum (with enumNames or
  oneOf[].title) becomes a dropdown instead of a value the user has to spell correctly;
  required becomes a marker; default pre-fills; minimum/maximum, minLength/maxLength,
  pattern and format become live constraints.
  Equally: which constructs cause the form to step aside. acp-ui declines
  if/then/else, dependentSchemas, allOf and discriminated oneOf, falling back to the plain
  text box with a reason. dependentRequired is supported. A server author choosing between
  two ways to express the same thing should know one of them renders and one does not.
  And the floor: a tool with no inputSchema, or with an untitled undescribed property bag,
  gets today's text box. Nothing breaks -- it just stays as opaque as it is now.

The doc should be honest that acp-ui is the first client to read this and that its exact
rendering rules are its own, not ours; what python-acp guarantees is the channel and the
verbatim pass-through, not any particular widget.
design:
Where: a new docs/tool-schema-contract.md, linked from README.md's docs list (alongside the interop runbook and compliance matrix) and from ARCHITECTURE.md. NOT a co-located module doc -- docs-check requires those to pair 1:1 with a src/python_acp/*.py file, and this describes a wire contract spanning commands.py, turn_mcp_router.py and mcp_tools.py rather than any one module. commands.md and turn_mcp_router.md should link *to* it rather than duplicate it.

Depends on pyacp-ma2 and must not land before it. capabilities.py's manifest comment states the rule this repo already lives by -- advertise in the same commit as the feature, never ahead of it -- and a document telling MCP authors their schemas are rendered, published while we still discard them, is that same mistake in prose. It is worse than the capability case, because a server author who acts on it changes their code for nothing.

Write it as a contract, not a tutorial: what we guarantee, what we do not, and what a reader on each side gets for participating. The acp-ui field-notes page is the model for tone -- every claim tied to what actually happens on the wire.
acceptance_criteria: docs/tool-schema-contract.md exists and covers both audiences: the _meta key and its guarantees for ACP clients, and the schema fields that become UI for MCP server authors, including which constructs are not rendered. Linked from README.md and ARCHITECTURE.md; commands.md and turn_mcp_router.md point to it. Every claim about emitted behaviour matches what pyacp-ma2 actually shipped. make lint && make docs-check && make test pass.
notes:
Prompted by acp-ui implementing the client half now, so the two documents will be
readable side by side: theirs tells agents what to send, this one tells clients what we
send and tells MCP servers why their schema quality is suddenly visible to a human. Their
docs/agent-integration.md is rendered at
https://claude.ai/code/artifact/c8a3af41-643c-4ccf-9f53-b643a35f2df7 and is the source for
the 'what acp-ui renders' and 'what acp-ui declines' lists -- cite it as theirs and let it
own those, since its rendering rules can change without ours changing.

Existing material to draw on rather than rewrite: commands.md's three-shapes table
(properties with entries / properties: {} / no inputSchema at all) already makes the
'omitted is not the same as empty' argument in its own voice, and tool_command_hint
(commands.py:912) is the proof we can read these schemas at all.

Related: pyacp-8lp pins the rest of the acp-ui checklist as tests.

title: Pin the acp-ui client-integration contract as a test
description:
acp-ui's docs/agent-integration.md (rendered as the "ACP Agent Field Notes" page) lists
seven things an agent should do so its sessions render well. python-acp already satisfies
six of them -- but each is satisfied incidentally, by whichever module happened to get it
right, and nothing states them as a contract that a refactor would be caught breaking.

Currently satisfied, and where:

  toolCallId on session/request_permission -- PermissionBroker.request_for() builds the
    ToolCallUpdate from the tracker (turn_mcp_router.py:1491), so the id matches the call
    it gates. Nothing asserts that; a future call site passing an explicit tool_call=
    would drop it silently.
  reject_always offered -- _PERMISSION_OPTIONS (turn_mcp_router.py:535) is
    default_permission_options() plus reject_for_session. Regression risk is the SDK
    changing its defaults under us.
  tool_call before the work -- the ToolCall notification goes out at
    turn_mcp_router.py:1206, and in_progress only at :1256. An ordering change reads as a
    hung agent in the client, which no unit test would notice.
  kind from the closed vocabulary -- ToolCatalogue.kind() (mcp_tools.py:141) returns a
    typed ToolKind and never raises.
  byte-identical prompt echo -- _echo_prompt (turn_mcp_router.py:666) emits block text
    verbatim. Any future normalisation (trim, re-wrap) makes acp-ui render the prompt
    twice.
  rawInput / rawOutput -- turn_mcp_router.py:1208 / :1289.
  locations -- Invocation.locations, turn_mcp_router.py:1209.

Also confirmed correct and worth an assertion: fs/read_text_file and fs/write_text_file
are gated on clientCapabilities.fs via Gate.READ_TEXT_FILE / Gate.WRITE_TEXT_FILE
(turn_mcp_router.py:1010, :1130, :1309, :1345), and mcpCapabilities.{http,sse,acp} are
advertised false (capabilities.py:186-208) to match the stdio-only reality -- acp-ui
filters the user's MCP server list by exactly those, so understating or overstating them
withholds servers or produces a visible "MCP is broken".

The ask is a single test module that asserts the above against a recorded turn -- the
tests/interop/ transcript is the natural place, since it is already a whole session
captured in both directions -- with each assertion carrying the one-line reason from the
client's side. Not new behaviour: a statement of an external contract we currently keep
by luck.
design:
Assert, do not re-implement. No production change is expected; if an assertion fails, the fix is in production code, not the test.

Prefer asserting against the existing interop transcript or a golden transcript over reaching into internals -- the contract is about what crosses the wire, and a test that inspects _PERMISSION_OPTIONS directly would keep passing if the wire stopped carrying it.
acceptance_criteria: One test module asserts each contract item above against a real turn; each assertion names the client-side consequence of breaking it; make lint && make docs-check && make test pass.
