description:
`_commands_for` (turn_mcp_router.py:1589) announces one AvailableCommand per
MCP tool, and `tool_command_hint` (commands.py:912) already reads that tool's
`inputSchema` -- its `properties`, `type` and `required` -- to build the hint.
It then discards the structure, because ACP's only argument shape is
`UnstructuredCommandInput`: a single display string a client cannot validate
against, as the comment at turn_mcp_router.py:441 says.

A client that had the schema could render a real form: typed inputs, required
markers, ranges, and enum values as dropdowns instead of a value the user has
to know and type correctly. acp-ui wants exactly this (acpui-26v).

`AvailableCommand` already carries `_meta` (schema.py:4330) -- ACP's own
extensibility point, explicitly reserved for this. So the change is small:

    AvailableCommand(
        name=f"{server}/{name}",
        description=...,
        input=...,
        field_meta={"python-acp/tool": {
            "server": server,
            "tool": name,
            "inputSchema": tool.get("inputSchema"),
        }},
    )

The hint stays exactly as it is. `_meta` is additive and a client that ignores
it sees no change at all, which is the property that makes this safe to ship
ahead of any client.

Namespaced key because ACP says implementations MUST NOT make assumptions
about `_meta` values: an unnamespaced `inputSchema` would be a land grab on a
shared dict.

WORTH MEASURING BEFORE MERGING: `available_commands_update` is re-announced
every turn. Schemas are much larger than hints, so this multiplies the size of
a per-turn notification by something like the ratio of a schema to its
one-line summary. If that is material, options are (a) send `_meta` only in
the once-per-session announcement from `available_commands`, at the cost of
the per-turn list disagreeing with it, or (b) gate it on a client capability
advertised in `clientCapabilities._meta`, which is the more correct answer and
the more work. Measure first; do not pre-optimise a payload nobody has weighed.
design: Emit only. python-acp keeps deciding what a valid call is -- coerce_arguments (commands.py:638) stays the authority, and a client-side form is a convenience that must not become a trust boundary. A form that validated locally and skipped the agent's checks would be a regression in exactly the direction that matters.
acceptance_criteria: Per-tool AvailableCommands carry _meta['python-acp/tool'].inputSchema matching what tools/list returned; a tool that publishes no schema omits the key rather than sending null-shaped noise; the hint string is unchanged; existing tests still pass; payload size impact measured and recorded on the issue.
notes:
Rationale and the full client-side contract are written up in acp-ui's repo at docs/agent-integration.md (commit 684a990), section 2. It states the namespacing convention, what acp-ui reads out of a schema, which JSON Schema constructs it declines to render, and the per-turn payload cost this bead has to measure.

--- PAYLOAD MEASUREMENT (the bead's precondition for merging) ---

Serialised available_commands_update, compact JSON, with and without field_meta:

  fixture (3 tiny tools)      1,428 B -> 1,797 B   +369 B   1.26x
  realistic (3 real tools)    1,702 B -> 3,595 B  +1,893 B  2.11x

Whole-notification ratios understate it: the seven built-ins are a fixed floor that
carries no _meta and dilutes the average. Per entry:

  Demo/echo             83 ->   235 B   (+152)
  Demo/wipe             86 ->   194 B   (+108)
  Demo/plain            98 ->   207 B   (+109)
  files/read_file      155 ->   703 B   (+548)
  files/search         192 ->   891 B   (+699)
  files/create_issue   194 ->   840 B   (+646)

The 'realistic' set is three tools shaped after common filesystem / search / issue-tracker
MCP servers -- titles, descriptions, enums with enumNames, defaults, minimum/maximum,
minLength/maxLength, format, array items. That is the case this feature exists for, and
the fixture's near-empty schemas are the floor, not the expectation.

A schema-carrying entry is ~4.5x its bare self, ~+630 B for a real tool.

DECISION: shipped ungated. ~630 B/tool puts a 20-tool session near 13 KB per turn, which
no transport this bridge uses notices, and neither escape is free -- option (a) makes the
per-turn list disagree with the session-open one, which is the exact property _commands_for
exists to guarantee, and (b) is a capability negotiation bought before anyone is paying.
Both are recorded in turn_mcp_router.md so the next person facing a real bill finds them.
Measurement script: scratchpad/measure.py (not committed; it is a one-off).
close_reason: Closed

title: A positional argument to a tool command is refused with the value echoed back as a parameter name
description:
`/Demo/echo foo bar` is refused by `_parse_flags` (commands.py:462) with:

  /Demo/echo: unexpected argument 'foo'. Every parameter is named: `--foo <value>`.

Two problems, one message:

1. The suggested flag is built from the *token that failed*, which is the user's
   VALUE, not a parameter name. It reads as advice to run `/Demo/echo --foo bar`,
   which is wrong and fails differently (there is no parameter --foo).
2. It never names the tool's actual parameters, even though they are one lookup
   away: `tool_command_hint` already renders them from `inputSchema` for the
   palette entry, and the router holds the `ToolCatalogue`.

Refusing the positional form is correct — MCP tool arguments are a named object,
so there is no position to map onto, and guessing is what `_resolve_server`
already refuses to do elsewhere. Only the message is wrong.

The obstacle is structural: `_parse_flags` runs inside `parse_command`, which is
pure parsing with no schema, and `_command_in` turns the CommandError into a
CommandRefused before any server is resolved. So the fix is to defer the
positional complaint for `/<server>/<tool>` commands to the router, where the
catalogue can name the real parameters.

Observed live in acp-ui at 08:17:11 on 2026-08-28, immediately after the
pyacp-acn hint work: the hint is now advertised, but a user who types
positionally anyway still gets the unhelpful message.
acceptance_criteria:
A positional argument to /<server>/<tool> is refused with a message naming the tool's real parameters, taken from its inputSchema, and a runnable example (e.g. `Try /Demo/echo --text foo`).
The failing token is never re-rendered as a --flag suggestion.
A tool with no schema, or no declared properties, still gets an honest message rather than an invented flag.
/invokeTool and the prompt commands keep working; whatever is shared with them stays shared.
Tests cover: positional token with a schema, without a schema, and in a session with several servers.
make lint && make docs-check && make test pass.
close_reason: Closed

title: [bug] A curly quote in a slash command is reported four tokens away from its cause
description:
`shlex.split` does not recognise `“` and `”` as quote characters, so a command a GUI
composer autocorrected is split at every space:

    typed : /invokeTool demo/echo --text “Hello from the GUI”
    tokens: ['/invokeTool', 'demo/echo', '--text', '“Hello', 'from', 'the', 'GUI”']

`--text` takes `“Hello`, and the next bare word is refused as a positional:

    /invokeTool: unexpected argument 'from'. Every parameter is named: `--from <value>`.

The message is correct and useless. It names token 4 when the cause is at token 3, and
`"` versus `“` is nearly invisible in a chat composer — the reader is sent looking at the
word `from`, which is not the problem.

Observed live in acp-ui. This is the third autocorrect substitution to break this
integration in one session (an em dash in the agent args was the first two), so it is a
recurring hazard of the surface rather than a one-off typo.

**Decided approach (user's call): detect and explain, do not accept.** Curly quotes are
not made into delimiters. `’` is an apostrophe far more often than a quote, so accepting
the single forms would corrupt ordinary text, and accepting only the double forms would
make the rule arbitrary. Parsing behaviour is unchanged; only the failure message gains a
sentence naming the real cause and showing the straight-quote form.
acceptance_criteria:
Tokenisation is UNCHANGED: no curly quote becomes a delimiter, and a command that parsed before parses identically.
When parsing raises CommandError and the raw command text contains a curly quote, the message names the curly quote as the likely cause and shows the same command with straight quotes.
The note is attached once, at the one place raw text becomes tokens — not per raise site.
A command containing a curly quote that parses fine (e.g. inside an already-straight-quoted value) gets no note.
The added text is markdown-safe per tests/test_markdown.py::assert_markdown_safe.
make lint && make docs-check && make test pass.
close_reason: Closed

title: start-ws.sh pre-launch failures are invisible to a client that hides stderr
description:
`scripts/start-ws.sh` can fail before it ever launches python — a missing venv
interpreter (`exit 1`), or `source .venv/bin/activate` failing under `set -e`. Both
paths speak only on stderr, and both happen *before* the `--log` branch writes its
`--- python-acp start <ts> ---` banner, so `--log` records nothing at all.

A client that swallows stderr therefore shows the operator an empty log and a bare
"agent process exited". Observed live: an acp-ui run at 21:34:18 left no banner in
logs/python-acp-ws.log, which is what made that particular failure undiagnosable
without interposing a separate tap process to capture stderr.

The `--log` path is the operator's one durable record. Anything that can kill the
script should reach it.
acceptance_criteria:
When --log is given, the banner is written (and the log dir created) BEFORE the venv check and activate, so every failure path after argument parsing lands in the log file.
A missing venv interpreter and a failing activate each write a diagnostic to the log as well as stderr.
The script still exits non-zero with the same codes.
stdout stays a clean protocol wire on every path — nothing new is printed to fd 1.
A test covers a missing-interpreter run with --log and asserts the log names the cause.
make lint && make docs-check && make test pass.
close_reason: Closed

title: [bug] start-ws.sh forwards empty arguments to argparse, turning a config typo into an opaque exit 2
description:
`scripts/start-ws.sh`'s catch-all `*)` branch appends every unrecognised token to
`cli_args`, including the empty string, which argparse then rejects:

    $ scripts/start-ws.sh '' --transport stdio --debug
    python -m python_acp.cli: error: unrecognized arguments:
    EXIT=2

The trailing message is blank, so nothing on screen names the cause.

Found in a live acp-ui session. acp-ui builds one shell string as
`{command} {args joined by space}` (src-tauri/src/agent.rs) and hands it to
`$SHELL -l -c`, so a blank row in its agent-config args list becomes a literal `''`
argument. The agent exited 2 before writing a byte to stdout; acp-ui reported it as
`transport closed: agent process exited`, which reads as a mid-session crash rather
than a launch failure. It cost four debugging rounds to identify.

An empty argument is never meaningful to the CLI, and dropping it costs nothing.
acceptance_criteria:
start-ws.sh drops empty arguments rather than forwarding them to the CLI.
A non-empty argument that merely looks odd is still forwarded untouched — the script stays a pass-through.
tests/test_start_ws.sh (or the existing script test) covers an empty argument in first, middle, and last position, and after `--`.
make lint && make docs-check && make test pass.
close_reason: Closed

title: Let an operator refuse client-supplied MCP servers
description:
pyacp-lx7 gave an operator a catalogue a client can SELECT from, but did not close the door it was partly motivated by: session/new's mcpServers is still accepted from anyone, so on a shared socket a client past the access key can still make this process spawn an arbitrary binary. The catalogue made selection AVAILABLE; it did not make supply refusable.

Decided permissive by the user 2026-08-27 when pyacp-lx7 was scoped, deliberately -- keeping mcpServers is fully backward compatible and stays strict ACP v1. This bead is the other half, as an opt-in an operator sets when binding somewhere shared.

WHY A FLAG AND NOT A DEFAULT. Refusing by default would break every client that names its own servers today, including tests/interop/client.py and a good part of the suite, and it would be wrong for the stdio transport, where the client SPAWNED this process and supplying its own config is the canonical ACP arrangement. The risk is specific to a long-lived socket with clients the operator did not start.

SHAPE: --no-client-mcp-servers (name to settle; --mcp-servers=catalogue-only is another reading). With it set, a session/new or session/fork carrying a non-empty mcpServers is -32602 naming the flag and pointing at the catalogue, rather than silently ignoring the list -- a session backed by fewer servers than asked for is the failure mode README already warns about for skip-invalid-items, and this must not add a second route to it.

OPEN QUESTIONS:
1. Does it apply to --transport stdio at all? Arguably meaningless there and worth refusing the combination at startup, or worth allowing so one config works everywhere.
2. Is an EMPTY mcpServers list still fine? It must be -- it is what a catalogue-only client sends, and every existing test sends it.
3. Does it belong in the catalogue FILE instead of argv, as a top-level key? One file to deploy rather than a file plus a flag.
design: agent._reject_unsupported_mcp_servers is already the one funnel every client-supplied list goes through, on both session/new and session/fork, so the refusal has one place to live. The flag reaches PythonAcpAgent the way catalogue does -- cli.py -> WebSocketAgentServer/serve_websocket -> agent, or via run_stdio's already-constructed agent.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Default behaviour is unchanged: no flag, client servers accepted, additive with the catalogue.
2. With the flag, a non-empty mcpServers on session/new or session/fork is -32602 naming the flag -- never ignored.
3. An empty list is still accepted with the flag set.
4. The refusal happens before the session is created, leaving nothing behind.
5. Documented in README's 'Or the agent brings them, and you select' section and in cli.md.
6. make lint && make docs-check && make test.

title: Announce commands for session/new and session/fork, after the response, via a stream observer
description:
acp-ui populates its slash-command palette from available_commands_update and wants it before the first prompt. pyacp-obt shipped that for session/load and session/resume; session/new and session/fork were left out because the client learns the minted id from the RESPONSE, and a notification emitted from inside the handler goes out first, naming a session the client has never seen.

That gap is closable without an extension method. acp.Connection._run_request (connection.py:187-190) is:
    payload = await self._execute_request(message)
    await self._transport.send(payload)
    self._notify_observers(StreamDirection.OUTGOING, payload)
so a STREAM OBSERVER runs strictly after the response bytes are on the wire. Observers are public API and reach us through run_agent(**connection_kwargs) -> AgentSideConnection -> Connection(observers=[...]). Proven by probe: initialize then session/new produced 'RESPONSE id=2 {sessionId: 11fe7e...}' followed by 'NOTIFY session/update available_commands_update' for that same id.

An observer sees both directions, so it records incoming id->method for session/new and session/fork and matches the outgoing RESPONSE by id -- a JSON-RPC response carries no method of its own. It must distinguish a response from an agent-originated REQUEST: both are outgoing and both carry an id, and the agent's own id counter is independent of the client's, so session/request_permission id=2 can collide with the client's session/new id=2. A response has result/error and no method.
design:
New module announcer.py (+ announcer.md, docs-check requires the sibling). It does NOT live in agent.py: agent.py's docstring states that nothing in it parses a request id or knows a transport exists, and an observer matching raw JSON-RPC frames is exactly that. It takes the announce callable (agent.announce_commands), not the agent, so it depends on nothing.

Both transports wire it, because transport_ws.md already records that the two must not diverge: serve_websocket and run_stdio each pass observers= to run_agent.

Never fatal, same policy as announce_commands: the observer swallows and logs, since it fires after the response and cannot fail the request anyway -- and a socket that closed between the response and the announcement is ordinary.
acceptance_criteria:
1. session/new and session/fork each emit available_commands_update AFTER their response, on both transports.
2. A test asserts the wire ORDER, not just presence.
3. A test covers the id-collision case: an agent-originated outgoing request whose id matches a pending session/new must not be mistaken for the response.
4. A failed or errored session/new announces nothing.
5. agent.py:new_session's 'no announcement here, and it is not an oversight' comment, announce_commands' docstring, and agent.md's 'Commands are announced where the client already knows the session id' section are corrected -- all three record the now-disproved 'cannot'.
6. make lint && make docs-check && make test.
close_reason: Implemented in announcer.py: a stream observer emits available_commands_update for session/new and session/fork after the SDK writes their response. Both transports wire it. 1091 tests pass; the three golden transcripts were re-recorded and read.

title: Launch targets another program can start: make stdio, and cwd-independence for run/debug
description:
The Makefile had no stdio target at all, and its two launch targets could only be started from the repo root — a blocker for an app that spawns the bridge itself.

Adds `make stdio` (ACP on make's own stdin/stdout, DEBUG=1 for --debug, LOG for the tee) and makes all three launch targets — run, debug, stdio — callable from any working directory via `make -f /path/to/python-acp/Makefile <target>`.

Two distinct failures were fixed, not one:
1. relative paths (scripts/, .venv/) resolving against the caller's cwd — fixed with a leading `cd $(MAKEFILE_DIR)` per shell command;
2. the `venv` PREREQUISITE resolving against the caller's cwd, which killed run/debug with "No rule to make target 'pyproject.toml'" before any recipe line ran. No chdir inside a recipe can fix that, so all three dropped the prerequisite and call $(ENSURE_VENV) after the chdir instead.

stdio additionally keeps every diagnostic off stdout (banner, and the bootstrap's own [venv] logging, folded onto stderr) because under --transport stdio stdout is the JSON-RPC wire, and mints no access key — a key guards a socket and there is no socket.

Also adds the clean-shutdown log line in transport_stdio.py. run_agent returns on EOF and nothing else, so the process was stopping silently; from a parent that is indistinguishable from a crash, and it was reported as 'the agent exits after initialize' when the parent was closing the pipe.
acceptance_criteria:
make stdio serves ACP on stdin/stdout; DEBUG=1 adds --debug; LOG=1/LOG=path tee diagnostics.
run, debug and stdio all start from an unrelated cwd via make -f, with no venv prerequisite on any of them.
Nothing but JSON-RPC reaches stdout under stdio, proven end to end.
A clean EOF shutdown logs 'client closed stdin; python-acp exiting' and exits 0.
tests/test_makefile_targets.py and tests/test_transport_stdio.py cover all of it; make lint, docs-check, stats-check and test pass.
close_reason: Shipped: make stdio, cwd-independent launch targets, clean-shutdown log line. Gates green (1078 tests).

title: Templated resources are invisible: /listResources never calls resources/templates/list
description:
`_list_resources` (turn_mcp_router.py:736) builds its catalogue from `list_resources`
alone. MCP publishes URI *templates* through a SEPARATE method -- `resources/templates/list`
-- with its own result key and field name: {"resourceTemplates": [{uriTemplate, name,
description, mimeType}]}. Note `uriTemplate`, not `uri`.

Nothing in MCPStdioClient wraps that method, so a server whose resources are all
templates (a filesystem server publishing file:///{path}, a database server publishing
db://{table}) is reported by /listResources as "0 resources on 1 server."

That is a confident WRONG PICTURE, not a missing feature, which is what makes it a bug
and not an enhancement. `_catalogue`'s `undeclared` bucket does not catch it either: such
a server DOES declare the `resources` capability, it just returns an empty resources/list
page. So the reader is told the server has nothing, when it has plenty to read.

Scope is the discovery half ONLY. Expanding a template into a concrete URI is client-side
RFC 6570 work and is deliberately split out -- see the blocked follow-up. A user who can
SEE `greeting://{name}` can already type `/resourceShow demo greeting://ada` today, which
is why discovery alone is worth shipping on its own.

FIXTURE NOTE, and it is load-bearing: tests/fixtures/mock_mcp_server.py currently
advertises the template `greeting://{name}` from `resource_for_page(0)` -- i.e. inside
`resources/list`, which is exactly the mistake this bead is about. Moving it to a
resources/templates/list branch will break tests/test_turn_mcp_router.py:2383
(test_list_resources_reports_uri_and_mime_type), which asserts `greeting://{name}` appears
in /listResources output. That test is currently asserting the wrong behaviour; it should
end up asserting the template shows in the templates section and a concrete resource shows
in the resources section.
design:
1. mcp_stdio.py: `list_resource_templates()` on `_list_all`, keyed "resourceTemplates".
   It is a list method, so it goes through `_list_all` -- cursor walk, repeated-cursor
   guard and _MAX_LIST_PAGES for free -- never a bare `request()`.
2. Capability gate: `resources` unlocks resources/list, resources/read AND
   resources/templates/list. No new capability to check, but a server declaring
   `resources` may still answer -32601 for templates specifically. Decide whether that
   is an error or an empty section -- an empty section is almost certainly right, since
   templates are optional within the capability.
3. Fixture: a resources/templates/list branch; move `greeting://{name}` there and give
   resource_for_page(0) a concrete URI.
4. turn_mcp_router._list_resources: second `_catalogue` pass, and
   render_resource_listing gains a templates section. Keep the two visually distinct --
   a template is not readable as printed, and rendering them in one flat list would
   invite exactly the /resourceShow that fails.
5. Docs: mcp_stdio.md Main Symbols, commands.md's primitive table, and narrow the
   mcp-protocol skill's "Templated resources are not reachable" divergence note again --
   after this it is only the expansion half that is missing.
acceptance_criteria: list_resource_templates() exists on _list_all and is covered by a fixture-backed test; /listResources shows a server's URI templates in a section distinct from its concrete resources; a server that answers -32601 for resources/templates/list still lists its concrete resources; the mcp-protocol skill's divergence note is narrowed to expansion only.

title: Make /promptInvoke work once a model exists
description:
`/promptInvoke` ships refusing (pyacp-tc5): it validates its arguments, then says that acting on an expanded prompt needs a model and this bridge has none (decision D1). The refusal hands back the equivalent `/promptShow`, which does work, since expanding a prompt is a template substitution the MCP server performs.

The user's plan is that an upcoming epic introduces an LLM. When it lands, this is the command that changes meaning: `prompts/get` returns messages addressed to a model, and `/promptInvoke` should feed them to it rather than refusing.

WHAT IS ALREADY IN PLACE: parsing, server resolution, the `prompts` capability check, argument validation against the prompt's declared `arguments`, and the `InvokePrompt` dataclass that `execute` dispatches on. The refusal is raised in `McpToolRouterExecutor._expand_prompt` in turn_mcp_router.py, immediately after `prompt_arguments` and deliberately BEFORE `prompts/get` is called -- there is nothing to undo, only a branch to replace.

`NEEDS_A_MODEL` in commands.py is the sentence, in one place because it is said twice (the refusal and the palette hint). `PROMPT_INVOKE_HINT` also carries '(needs a model; see /promptShow)' and must lose it in the same commit, or the palette will keep advertising a limitation that no longer exists.
acceptance_criteria: /promptInvoke expands the prompt and acts on the messages rather than refusing; NEEDS_A_MODEL and the '(needs a model)' half of PROMPT_INVOKE_HINT are gone; the refusal test in tests/test_turn_mcp_router.py is replaced rather than deleted.

title: Track the ACP v2 draft, and the schema/SDK version drift behind it
description:
ACP published a **draft v2** on 2026-07-20 (announcement: https://agentclientprotocol.com/announcements/acp-v2-draft). It is a draft: upstream says "various pieces can, and will, change before stabilization" and tells implementers to gate it behind version negotiation and never default to it.

The stable wire `protocolVersion` remains **1**. `acp.PROTOCOL_VERSION == 1` in the pinned SDK, and upstream's own changelog note for 0.7.0 says "The Protocol version is already, and remains, `1`. This is just for the JSON Schema itself." The `schema/v1` vs `schema/v2` directories are codegen artifacts, NOT a wire break.

## Three versions that are not the same number

- ACP wire protocol: 1 (stable), 2 (draft)
- Rust crate / schema releases: 1.7.0 (2026-08-20)
- Python SDK `agent-client-protocol`: 0.12.1 (2026-08-16), the newest published

The Python SDK trails the schema line. Anything planned against a v2 feature must first
confirm the Python SDK actually models it. `acp/core.py:44` exposes the gate as
`use_unstable_protocol: bool = False` on the connection constructors; nothing in this
repo passes it, and this repo drives its own transport, so how that flag threads through
`transport_ws.py` / `transport_stdio.py` is unverified.

## What v2 actually changes

1. Prompt lifecycle -- `session/update` may fire outside a user-initiated turn; "idle" is
   signalled separately from the prompt response.
2. Message patching -- messages, tool calls and output get stable IDs with uniform patch
   semantics (omitted = unchanged, null = clear, value = replace, chunk = append).
3. Tool call content streams without buffering the whole payload.
4. Diffs -- `oldText`/`newText` replaced by structured file changes (add/delete/modify/
   move/copy/binary) plus an optional `git_patch`.
5. Permission requests -- required `title`, optional `description`, extensible `subject`,
   instead of hard-wiring to a tool call.
6. Forward compatibility -- unknown `_`-prefixed enum variants are accepted.

Items 2 and 3 touch this repo directly: `turn_mcp_router.py::_announce_tools` re-emits the
whole `available_commands` list every turn, which patch semantics would let us send as a
no-op; and `mcp_content.py` currently buffers tool output.

## What v2 does NOT change

Slash commands. `AvailableCommand` stays `{name, description, input?}` and
`AvailableCommandInput` stays a single `UnstructuredCommandInput {hint: str}`. Checked
three ways: the v2 announcement does not mention commands, the upstream changelog has no
command entries under any `(unstable-v2)` label, and the protocol docs still read
"Currently supports unstructured text input". So `commands.py`'s hand-rolled `--flag`
parser is not scaffolding waiting on a protocol feature -- it is the answer for the
foreseeable future.

## Correction worth recording

A widely circulated description of "ACP v2" -- stateless core, no initialize handshake,
per-request `_meta` capabilities, `server/discover`, `ttlMs`/`cacheScope`, `auth/login`
+ `auth/logout`, deprecating roots/sampling/logging, HTTP+SSE removal -- is **MCP**, not
ACP. `Mcp-Session-Id`, `structuredContent`, roots, sampling and `listChanged` are MCP
vocabulary, and date-named revisions (`2025-06-18`, which `mcp_stdio.py:22` pins) are
MCP's convention while ACP uses plain integers. Do not plan against it.

A third protocol also called ACP -- IBM/BeeAI's Agent *Communication* Protocol, the one
CLAUDE.md already warns about under the PyPI name `acp-sdk` -- merged into A2A under the
Linux Foundation and wound down. Unrelated to Zed's ACP.
acceptance_criteria:
- Re-check upstream when the Python SDK publishes a release past 0.12.1, and record whether v2 is modelled there at all.
- Determine whether `use_unstable_protocol` can thread through this repo's own transports, or whether it is only reachable via the SDK's stdio/http constructors.
- Confirm the stable wire version is still 1 before any release note claims a version.
- No production default changes to v2. Any v2 work stays behind negotiation, per upstream's own instruction.
- Leave `SUPPORTED_PROTOCOL_VERSIONS` a set. It is already the right shape for serving 1 and 2 at once.

title: Extension request so a NEW session can get its commands before the first turn
description:
Follow-up to pyacp-obt, which is implemented for session/load and session/resume (commit 6f987d1) and CANNOT be implemented for session/new or session/fork by notification. This bead is the remaining route.

THE CONSTRAINT, verified on the wire and worth not rediscovering:
- session/new and session/fork mint an id the client learns from the RESPONSE. A session/update emitted from inside the handler is sent FIRST and names a session the client has never heard of. Observed: 'NOTIFICATION session/update sessionId=2a9b...' then 'RESPONSE to id=1' carrying that same id.
- Emitting AFTER the response is not available in the SDK. acp.Connection._run_request (connection.py:187) awaits the handler and then does 'await self._transport.send(payload)'. There is no ordered outgoing queue -- each sender awaits the transport directly -- so a task scheduled from inside the handler RACES the reply rather than following it. Do not 'fix' this with create_task or a sleep.
- ACP carries no alternative: NewSessionResponse has session_id/modes/config_options/field_meta and no command field; LoadSessionResponse has modes/config_options. AvailableCommand (name, description, input) is only ever delivered by the available_commands_update session/update variant.

PROPOSED SHAPE: an extension REQUEST, which is deterministic because the client asks once it already holds the id. The SDK's extension channel is a LEADING UNDERSCORE, not '$/' (router.py:174 routes _foo to the handler registered by handle_extension_request; '$/' is LSP and the SDK has no concept of it -- an unknown '$/ping' notification produced a method_not_found traceback per ping until acp-ui dropped it). So: _session/available_commands, or _session/list_tools if the richer per-server shape is wanted.

DECISIONS NEEDED BEFORE CODING:
1. Does it return ACP AvailableCommand entries (name/description/hint, matching what turns announce and what a palette renders), or a richer per-server structure with MCP inputSchema and annotations that AvailableCommand structurally cannot carry? The first is consistent; the second is what a palette would need to show parameter specs, which is why /tools renders text today.
2. Does the agent ALSO answer it over stdio? ext_method currently answers -32601 by decision (pyacp-sld.2), and adding an extension request reopens that in a narrow way -- worth stating explicitly in the compliance matrix rather than by accident.
3. acp-ui has to send it; this is useless unilaterally.

RELATED CODE: agent.announce_commands (the load/resume half, with the ordering comment), McpToolRouterExecutor.available_commands, and _commands_for in turn_mcp_router.py, which is the one builder both callers share and which this should also use. commands.py owns /tools and /invokeTool, which is the existing human-facing answer to the same question.
notes:
PREMISE CORRECTED 2026-08-26. 'Emitting AFTER the response is not available in the SDK' is wrong, and the extension request may not be needed at all.

connection.py:187-190 reads:
    payload = await self._execute_request(message)
    await self._transport.send(payload)
    self._notify_observers(StreamDirection.OUTGOING, payload)

So a STREAM OBSERVER fires strictly after the response is on the wire. Observers are public: Connection.add_observer, or observers=[...] passed through run_agent's **connection_kwargs -> AgentSideConnection -> Connection. An observer sees both directions, so it can record incoming id->method and match the outgoing response by id (a JSON-RPC response carries no method of its own).

PROVEN by probe against a fake socket: initialize, then session/new, produced in order
  RESPONSE id=2 {sessionId: 11fe7e...}
  NOTIFY session/update {sessionId: 11fe7e..., availableCommands: []}
which is exactly the ordering the bead says is unreachable. What is still true is the narrower claim: emitting from INSIDE the handler is too early, and create_task from inside the handler races.

So the shape to build is probably (a) after all -- an observer-driven post-response announce for session/new and session/fork, reusing agent.announce_commands and _commands_for, with no new method and no acp-ui change. Wiring cost: serve_websocket and transport_stdio must both pass observers= to run_agent, and the observer needs the connection handle (agent.on_connect already receives it). Open question that survives: whether acp-ui wants richer per-server data than AvailableCommand can carry, which is the only remaining reason for an extension request.

Also update agent.py:541 announce_commands docstring and agent.md's 'Commands are announced where the client already knows the session id' section, both of which record the wrong 'cannot'.
close_reason: Not needed. pyacp-p8v closed the gap by notification instead: a stream observer announces available_commands_update after the session/new and session/fork responses, so no extension request and no client change. The bead's premise -- that emitting after the response is unavailable in the SDK -- was wrong; see its notes. Reopen only if a client wants more than AvailableCommand can carry (per-server grouping, MCP inputSchema, annotations); acp-ui displays name and description only, confirmed by the user 2026-08-27.

title: Surface MCP prompts (and resources) as ACP commands/context
description:
MCPStdioClient implements list_prompts/get_prompt (mcp_stdio.py:452-458) and list_resources/read_resource (460-500). All four have ZERO callers outside mcp_stdio.py, verified repo-wide; only list_tools (5) and call_tool (15) are wired up. So two of MCP's three server primitives are implemented at the client layer and reach no client.

WHY IT MATTERS: this bridge announces TOOLS as available_commands (server/tool), which is the non-conventional choice. In MCP's own model tools are model-controlled and PROMPTS are user-controlled -- prompts are the primitive designed to be surfaced as slash commands, and that is what Zed and Claude Desktop do with them. Our palette shows the model's callables where the convention shows the user's.

THE SHAPE PROBLEM, which is the real design question: MCP prompts carry named arguments ({name, description, required}), while ACP's AvailableCommand has only name/description plus an optional AvailableCommandInput whose single variant is UnstructuredCommandInput{hint} -- one free-text blob with a display hint. Named/required arguments cannot survive that squeeze without a convention (render the signature into the hint? require a JSON blob? decline prompts with required args?).

RESOURCES have no ACP listing at all: ACP carries resources only as content blocks INSIDE a prompt -- ResourceLink (uri/name/mime_type/size/...) and EmbeddedResource -- and embedded context is capability-gated (capabilities.py:181, promptCapabilities.embeddedContext, currently advertised false). There is no resources/list equivalent; the client supplies context, the agent does not enumerate it. So exposing MCP resources means deciding whether the AGENT ever offers them, which ACP does not really model.

Decide, in order: (1) do prompts appear as available_commands, alongside or instead of tools; (2) how prompt arguments map to the hint string; (3) whether resources surface at all, and if so as what. Coordinate with acp-ui. Related: pyacp-obt (on-demand tools listing) -- whatever populates the palette should settle prompts vs tools first, since it changes what the listing contains.

The mock fixture already serves a 'greeting' prompt with a required 'name' argument plus paged variants, so the test surface exists.
notes:
RESOLVED (2026-08-26). The three questions the description asked, decided by the user:

(1) DO PROMPTS APPEAR AS available_commands? The VERBS do; individual prompts do not. MCP keeps tools, prompts and resources in three separate namespaces, so one server may legally publish a tool and a prompt both called 'greeting'. Per-item palette entries would have needed a naming rule to keep those apart and the entry that lost would silently shadow the other; /listPrompts answers the same question without inventing one. Tools keep their existing server/tool entries.

(2) HOW DO PROMPT ARGUMENTS MAP TO THE HINT? They do not have to. The shape problem was smaller than filed: MCP types prompts/get's arguments as {[key: string]: string}, so there is no inputSchema, no declared type, and nothing to coerce. Prompt arguments are NAMED STRINGS and a command line carries named strings natively. prompt_arguments() checks names against the prompt's declared arguments and required-ness, and leaves values alone. The AvailableCommandInput hint is a display string, as it is for every other command.

(3) DO RESOURCES SURFACE? Yes -- /listResources and /resourceShow. The user's ruling on the proposed resourceShow/resourceInvoke pair: 'resource/read is the same intent, execute the underlying code', so they collapse into one verb. Unlike prompts there is no model-shaped second half to defer; resources/read IS the operation.

THE sld.2 REVERSAL, which the correction note said was the real ask: REOPENED AND REVERSED for prompt and resource CONTENT. /promptShow and /resourceShow deliver it to a client through this bridge. Recorded as a deliberate reversal in commands.md, commands.py's docstring, the commit message, and the acp-protocol skill -- not slipped in. What still stands from sld.2: no MCP method on the ACP wire, no process-wide server to address, nothing bypassing session/new, and ext_method still answers -32601.

/promptInvoke ships REFUSING, per the user, on the authenticate -32000 principle: a client discovers a boundary, not an absence. It validates arguments first and refuses before prompts/get, so a wrong argument is reported as a wrong argument. pyacp-9d5 owns making it work when the LLM epic lands.

ALSO LANDED: mcp_stdio keeps the server's initialize capability block (supports()), because MCP's rule runs both ways and an undeclared prompts capability otherwise surfaces as a -32601 naming a method nobody typed. Filed pyacp-ito for read_resource's non-spec 'arguments' param, which this work gave its first real caller.


--- ORIGINAL CORRECTION NOTE, restored (it was overwritten by the note above; reproduced verbatim for the record) ---

CORRECTION to the description: this is not simply an unfilled gap. The acp-protocol skill records a DECISION (pyacp-sld.2/sld.3) that a client does not reach through this bridge to read an MCP prompt or resource -- 'ACP's model is that the agent uses those internally', and reopening it is the ask, not filling a hole. So the live question is narrower than filed: may the agent CONSUME prompts internally and surface them as commands (arguably yes, same as it consumes tools), versus exposing prompts/get and resources/read to clients (decided no). The argument-shape problem stands either way.


Correction: the /promptInvoke follow-up is pyacp-r44 (an earlier line in these notes and the close reason said pyacp-9d5, which is a different issue).
close_reason: Implemented on main (5a3c497). Five commands, decisions recorded in notes; follow-ups pyacp-9d5 (promptInvoke when the LLM epic lands) and pyacp-ito (read_resource's non-spec arguments param).

title: On-demand tools listing, without starting a turn
description:
acp-ui wants to populate a tool palette before the first prompt. Today the only way to learn a session's tools is to start a turn: turn_mcp_router._announce_tools emits available_commands at the start of every session/prompt, gated by the announce-tools config option.

PROTOCOL FACTS (SDK 0.12.1, checked):
- ACP has no tools/list and no MCP service listing. NewSessionResponse carries session_id/modes/config_options/field_meta; LoadSessionResponse carries modes/config_options. Neither mentions tools or servers.
- The only tool surface in the protocol is AvailableCommand (name, description, input, field_meta), carried by the available_commands_update session/update notification. It is a FLAT command list -- no server identity, no MCP input schema, no annotations. Our server/tool naming is a convention this bridge invented to smuggle server identity through 'name'.
- mcp/connect, mcp/message, mcp/disconnect are CLIENT_METHODS (agent->client), for the ACP-as-MCP-transport case behind mcpCapabilities.acp. They are not an enumeration API, and this bridge advertises acp/http/sse all false.

OPTIONS:
(a) Cheapest, no new method: emit the available_commands session/update right after session/new (and load/resume/fork), not only at turn start. A session/update notification is legal at any time, so no extension is needed and acp-ui needs no new call. Costs one tools/list per server at session creation; should presumably respect announce-tools=false.
(b) An extension REQUEST, e.g. _session/list_tools, via the SDK's underscore extension channel (router.py routes _foo to handle_extension_request). Needed only if acp-ui wants more than name+description -- per-server grouping, MCP input schemas, annotations -- which available_commands cannot express.

(a) likely covers the palette; (b) only if richer data is actually wanted. Needs an acp-ui decision before implementing.

Caching note: listings are deliberately uncached across turns -- honest caching needs notifications/tools/list_changed handling (see mcp_tools.py).
notes:
IMPLEMENTED PARTIALLY, and option (a) does NOT cover session/new -- a design flaw in the bead's premise, found by test_two_clients_are_served_at_once_each_with_its_own_agent.

Shipped: agent.announce_commands() emits available_commands_update from session/load and session/resume, where the CLIENT SUPPLIED the session id and can place the update. A reconnecting client gets its palette without taking a turn. Optional on the executor (getattr, D3 swappability) and never fatal (a failed tools/list is logged, not raised).

NOT shipped, and cannot be as filed: session/new and session/fork. Both mint an id the client learns from the RESPONSE, so a notification sent first names a session it has never heard of -- verified on the wire: NOTIFICATION session/update sessionId=2a9b... arrives BEFORE RESPONSE to id=1 carrying that same id. Sending it after the response is not available either: acp.Connection._run_request awaits the handler and then writes the response, with no ordered send queue, so a task scheduled inside the handler races the reply. NewSessionResponse has no command field (sessionId/modes/configOptions only) and ACP has no method to ask.

So for a NEW session the remaining routes are: (i) an ACP change adding commands to NewSessionResponse, (ii) option (b), an extension request like _session/available_commands that the client sends once it holds the id -- deterministic, small, no ordering hazard, or (iii) a client that tolerates updates for an unknown session, which is not a protocol guarantee and should not be designed around. (ii) is the recommendation; needs an acp-ui decision.
close_reason: Implemented for session/load and session/resume in 6f987d1. The session/new half is not implementable by notification (ordering constraint recorded in the issue notes and in pyacp-mth), so the remaining work is pyacp-mth: an extension request the client makes once it holds the id.

title: Name ping_interval/ping_timeout explicitly in the WS transport
description:
transport_ws.py calls websockets.serve() without ping_interval or ping_timeout, so the WebSocket keepalive is an unstated inheritance of the library default (20s/20s in websockets 17.0.1).

Why it matters: ACP defines no ping method -- 38 routed methods in SDK 0.12.1, none a heartbeat, and no $/ prefix concept (that is LSP). Keepalive is therefore a transport concern, which the SDK itself demonstrates in its HTTP/SSE transport via SSE_KEEPALIVE_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 15.0, 'kept in sync with the TypeScript reference so intermediaries do not time out an otherwise-healthy but quiet stream'.

acp-ui removed its $/ping notification (which was logging a method_not_found traceback per ping here) and now relies on server pings, naming ping_interval server-side as the remedy. That makes our interval part of the client-facing contract while it lives in no code or doc of ours. Runtime deps are exact-pinned in this repo because they are protocol surface; a websockets bump could change this default silently and nothing would fail.

Acceptance: named constants in transport_ws.py passed explicitly to serve(), the 20s-vs-SDK-15s choice reasoned in the comment, transport_ws.md updated, and a test that fails if the kwargs stop being passed.
notes: Done: _PING_INTERVAL_SECONDS/_PING_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (20.0/20.0) named in transport_ws.py and passed to serve(); reasoning comment cites the SDK's SSE_KEEPALIVE_INTERVAL_SECONDS=15.0 precedent; transport_ws.md section added; two tests -- one patches the constants to 7.5/3.25 and reads them off the real server-side connection (mutation-checked: fails when the kwargs are deleted), one bounds the shipped values. Note for review: asserting the shipped 20.0 does NOT work as a test, since websockets' own default is also 20.
close_reason: Implemented: explicit ping_interval/ping_timeout with reasoning, docs, and a mutation-checked test.

title: check_docs and code_stats skip .venv but not .venv311, so they walk matrix-leg venvs
description:
Both scripts filter with "part in SKIP_PARTS" where SKIP_PARTS contains the literal ".venv". That is an exact match on a path component, so a matrix-leg venv -- ".venv311", ".venv312", the arrangement .gitignore documents at line 155 and CLAUDE.md tells people to create by overriding VENV_DIR -- is not skipped at all. Neither is .pytest_cache.

Two consequences, one cosmetic and one not:

  * code_stats.py counts vendored markdown as ours. Today that is pip/_vendor/idna/LICENSE.md twice plus .pytest_cache/README.md: 3 files, 70 lines, inside a reported 34 files / 7,518 lines.
  * check_docs.py VALIDATES RELATIVE LINKS inside third-party markdown. A dependency shipping a .md whose link does not resolve from its installed location fails "make docs-check", and the error names a file nobody in this repo wrote. A CI failure with no local cause is the expensive kind.

Found while adding a per-file markdown breakdown to STATISTICS.md, which made the stray files visible for the first time -- the aggregate had been hiding them.
design: One predicate, defined once in check_docs.py and imported by code_stats.py -- they are both answering 'is this file ours', and two copies is how they drift apart. Prefix match for venv directories rather than an ever-growing literal list, plus the tool caches .gitignore already names.
acceptance_criteria: A path under .venv311/ is skipped by both scripts; .pytest_cache is skipped; a test asserts it so the exact-match bug cannot return; make lint docs-check test green
close_reason: Closed

title: Document that the WebSocket socket is unauthenticated and must not face an untrusted network
description:
README's Container usage section says to pass --host 0.0.0.0 and explains why (127.0.0.1 inside a container is reachable only from inside it) but never says what binding every interface exposes. There is no security note anywhere in the README, and a reader following the container recipe on a machine with a public interface publishes an agent that runs arbitrary commands on request.

Wanted: a short security section stating the threat model plainly -- session/new spawns commands named by the client, so whoever can reach the port can run them as the bridge's user -- plus what the access key does and does not cover (no TLS, so the key crosses the wire in the URL; use a tunnel or a reverse proxy for anything beyond a trusted LAN).

title: Publish a multi-arch container image (amd64 + arm64/v8) for Raspberry Pi
description:
The container image is built single-arch, native to whatever runs the build. pyacp-8ub measured it on linux/arm64 locally while publish-artifacts.yml builds it on ubuntu-latest (amd64), so the released image runs on x86 only and will not start on a Raspberry Pi.

SCOPE DECIDED WITH THE USER:
- Platforms: linux/amd64 + linux/arm64/v8. That covers Pi 3, 4, 5 and Zero 2 W on 64-bit Raspberry Pi OS, which has been the default since 2022.
- Built by CI on release, not by a local target run from someone's laptop.

ARMv8.2-A NEEDS NO SEPARATE BUILD, and cannot have one. Verified against the registry: python:3.11-slim publishes amd64, arm/v5, arm/v7, arm64/v8, 386, ppc64le, riscv64, s390x -- there is no arm64/v8.2, in OCI or on Docker Hub. ARMv8.2-A is a superset of ARMv8-A, so a linux/arm64/v8 image runs natively on a Pi 5 Cortex-A76. A distinct v8.2 build would only pay off if we compiled native code with -march=armv8.2-a; we ship py3-none-any and consume pydantic-core as a prebuilt manylinux aarch64 wheel targeting baseline ARMv8-A.

OUT OF SCOPE, with reasons:
- linux/arm/v7 (32-bit Pi OS). Viable -- pydantic-core ships manylinux_2_17_armv7l so it installs from a wheel -- but a third QEMU-emulated leg for a shrinking install base. Revisit on demand.
- Pi Zero / Pi 1 (ARMv6). Not reachable: python:3.11-slim has no arm/v6 (only v5 and v7) and pydantic-core publishes no armv6 or armv5 wheel, so it would mean compiling Rust on an ARM11.
design:
Containerfile needs no arch conditionals -- FROM python:3.11-slim resolves per-platform and nothing in it is arch-specific.

scripts/container_image.py grows a --platform flag. The two engines differ: docker buildx takes --platform a,b with --output type=oci; podman builds into a --manifest then pushes it to oci-archive. Command CONSTRUCTION is unit-testable through the injected runner already used for the stale-save tests; end-to-end multi-arch cannot be verified in the sandbox, which is why CI owns the real build.

Single-platform stays the default so existing behaviour and the skip logic from pyacp-t4y are untouched.
acceptance_criteria:
- container_image.py builds a multi-platform image via buildx or podman manifest
- PLATFORMS knob, defaulting to current single-platform behaviour
- publish-artifacts.yml builds amd64+arm64 with QEMU on release
- the released artifact is consumable on a Pi
- tests cover command construction for both engines and both modes
- docs state plainly that arm64 covers ARMv8.2-A, so nobody adds a v8.2 leg later
- make lint && make docs-check && make test pass
close_reason: Releases now build linux/amd64 + linux/arm64 under QEMU via buildx and attach a multi-platform OCI archive. arm64 covers Pi 3/4/5 and Zero 2 W on 64-bit Pi OS including the Pi 5's ARMv8.2-A, which is a superset of ARMv8-A and has no OCI platform of its own -- verified against the python:3.11-slim manifest list. PLATFORMS knob, RELEASE_PLATFORMS single source of truth read by the workflow via print-release-platforms. 17 new tests; single-arch-fallback and bogus-v8.2-platform guards both mutation-verified. arm/v7 excluded as a future one-liner, ARMv6 excluded as unreachable.

title: container-image: distinguish 'no engine' from 'engine unreachable', and stop failing open
description:
podman 6.1.0 is now installed on the dev machine, which broke two assumptions in the container-image target.

1) HARD FAILURE WHERE THERE WAS A SKIP. The recipe guards with 'command -v podman || command -v docker'. That now succeeds, so the build runs -- and dies, because the sandbox cannot reach the podman VM over ssh://core@127.0.0.1:<port> (loopback egress is not in the sandbox allowlist, and the user has ruled out exposing the socket). 'make container-image' exits 125 and 'make package', which depends on it, is broken in the sandbox.

2) THE RECIPE FAILS OPEN. build and save are joined by ';' not '&&', so save runs even after build fails. Today both fail so it is loud. On a machine holding a stale python-acp:local from an earlier run, a failed build would be followed by a SUCCESSFUL save of the stale image and the target would exit 0 having packaged the wrong container. This is the same fail-open class CLAUDE.md already calls out for docs-check.

The release path is where 2) bites hardest: publish-artifacts.yml runs 'make container-image' and then globs dist/*.tar into the GitHub release. A silent skip or a stale save ships a bad release with no signal.
design:
Move the conditional logic out of the Makefile recipe into scripts/container_image.py, following the precedent CLAUDE.md sets for scripts/venv_bootstrap.py ('the rules are conditional in ways make expresses badly'). That also makes it testable, which a recipe is not -- and per repo culture a gate that can report success by doing nothing needs a test.

Three-state detection replaces the two-state 'command -v': no engine installed / engine present but unreachable (probe it, do not just look it up on PATH) / engine ready. Join build and save with && so a failed build can never save a stale image.
acceptance_criteria:
- scripts/container_image.py owns detection, probe, build, and save
- 'engine unreachable' is a distinct, named outcome from 'no engine installed'
- a failed build can never produce or preserve a container tar
- REQUIRE_CONTAINER=1 turns any skip into a hard error; publish-artifacts.yml sets it
- 'make container-image' and 'make package' both succeed in the sandbox again
- tests/test_container_image.py covers all three states and the stale-save regression
- make lint && make docs-check && make test all pass
close_reason: scripts/container_image.py now probes the engine (<engine> version) instead of trusting PATH, giving three states; 'installed but unreachable' skips with a message naming the fix. REQUIRE_CONTAINER=1 makes any skip fatal and publish-artifacts.yml sets it. build/save ordered with a failed build deleting any stale tar. 15 tests, both regressions mutation-verified. make container-image and make package work in the sandbox again.

title: The acp-protocol and mcp-protocol skill files still describe elicitation as unimplemented; the sandbox cannot write .claude/skills
description:
pyacp-8bv.4 landed elicitation forwarding and corrected the docs everywhere it could reach, but .claude/skills/ is on the sandbox deny list, so the two skill files still carry claims that are now wrong. They are read BEFORE any change to either protocol surface, which makes a stale one more expensive than a stale doc.

notes: discovered-from: pyacp-8bv.4. Blocked on write access, not on knowledge: the exact edits are above. A human with an editor, or a session whose sandbox allows .claude/skills, can apply them directly.
close_reason: Not blocked after all: the sandbox deny list on .claude/skills binds Bash, not the Edit tool. Both skill files now describe elicitation as implemented, name elicitation/create as the ACP method it forwards to, describe clientCapabilities.elicitation as a container of two markers, and document MalformedServerRequest -> -32602 plus the off-loop server-request dispatch. Also added backend_responder to the mcp-protocol capability section and elicitation.py to its trigger list.

title: mcp-protocol skill still documents the pre-pyacp-pb7 capability block and version pin
description:
pyacp-pb7 moved the pinned MCP revision to 2025-06-18 (accepting 2024-11-05 back), replaced the hardcoded 'capabilities: {}' with MCPClientCapabilities, and made mcp_registry declare and answer roots/list. .claude/skills/mcp-protocol/SKILL.md and spec-versions.md were NOT updated with it: the agent sandbox denies writes under .claude/skills, so the edits could not be applied in the same commit. The skill is now actively misleading on four points.

SKILL.md, 'Capabilities are a promise you must keep': says 'We send "capabilities": {} — literally nothing. That is currently a lie by omission'. False now. Replace with: MCPClientCapabilities is the block; MCPStdioClient.client_capabilities is where a caller sets it; empty by default because a client with no on_server_request handler can answer nothing. title: Call fs/read_text_file and fs/write_text_file, gated on client capability
description:
Consume the client's filesystem methods rather than touching the filesystem directly, so the client stays in control of what is read and written.

Gate on the clientCapabilities captured at initialize (Phase 1.4) and define the fallback when the client does not offer fs -- direct filesystem access, or refusal. That choice interacts with Phase 2.5's containment rule, which is where the directory boundary is enforced.

read_text_file takes optional line and limit parameters; support them rather than always reading whole files.
acceptance_criteria: Both methods called through the client when advertised; line and limit honored on read; behavior with no fs capability is defined, documented, and tested; paths respect Phase 2.5's containment rule; a client that errors on the call does not crash the turn.
notes:
pyacp-3rw.4 settled the containment rule this bead enforces. Do not re-derive it:

    from python_acp.paths import require_contained
    resolved = require_contained(path, session.roots, "fs/read_text_file path")

- session.roots is (cwd, *additional_directories), already validated absolute and
  lexically normalised at the edge in agent.py.
- require_contained returns the RESOLVED path; use it. Re-deriving from the original
  string would open something the check never saw.
- Both sides resolve symlinks. A link inside cwd pointing at /etc/shadow is refused; a
  link inside pointing back inside is allowed; a declared root that is itself a link is
  still a live boundary. A prefix match is NOT containment. Empty roots permits nothing.
- PathConstraintError subclasses ValueError, so errors.to_request_error already answers
  -32602 with the reason in data. No special case needed.

KNOWN LIMIT this bead inherits and may need to close: containment is a CHECK, NOT A LOCK.
Resolution happens at check time, so a path that passes can become a symlink out of the
tree a microsecond later (TOCTOU). Closing it needs the fd actually opened -- openat /
O_NOFOLLOW -- which belongs with the code doing the opening, i.e. here. Documented in
src/python_acp/paths.md under "What this does not promise".
pyacp-hnk.1: gating lives on the turn seam, not at each call site. Start every client call with context.require(Gate.X) from python_acp.turns -- READ_TEXT_FILE / WRITE_TEXT_FILE (two INDEPENDENT booleans under fs; a read grant must never satisfy a write), TERMINAL (one boolean for all five terminal/* methods, no per-method granularity exists), ELICITATION (advertised by presence of an empty marker model, so 'is not None', not bool(model)). UngatedClientCallError is a RuntimeError -> -32603 because an ungated call is our conformance bug. A client that declared nothing may be called for nothing. See src/python_acp/turns.md.

RESOLVED (pyacp-8bv.2, in progress): the open question in the description -- "define the
fallback when the client does not offer fs: direct filesystem access, or refusal" -- is
answered REFUSAL. There is no direct-filesystem fallback and there will not be one.
Settled by pyacp-hnk.1's ClientGates ("Absent capabilities mean **no** ... which is the
only safe reading") and by this bead's own opening sentence: opening a file behind the
client's back defeats "so the client stays in control of what is read and written".

HOW the refusal is produced matters and is also settled: branch on context.allows(gate)
at PARSE time and refuse the turn with TurnResult.refused() before anything runs.
Do NOT route the ordinary no-capability case through context.require(gate) --
UngatedClientCallError is a RuntimeError -> -32603 and means OUR conformance bug, so it
would report us as broken for a client's perfectly conforming absence of a capability.
require() is kept at the call site as an assertion, where a shut gate really would mean
the parse-time check was missing.

ALSO FOUND: the KNOWN LIMIT this bead was told it "may need to close" (containment is a
check, not a lock; TOCTOU) CANNOT be closed here, and the premise that it could was
wrong. paths.md said the openat/O_NOFOLLOW fix "belongs with the code doing the opening,
i.e. Phase 4.2". Phase 4.2 opens nothing -- the CLIENT opens the file, over the wire.
The mitigation available on this side is sending the resolved path so the client is not
asked to re-walk links already walked; the rest is the client's fs/* implementation.
paths.py, paths.md and turn_mcp_router.md now say so.
close_reason: All acceptance criteria met; merged to main. fs/read_text_file and fs/write_text_file called through the client, gated with allows() at parse time (refusal) and require() at the call site as our-invariant assertion; line/limit honored; containment via require_contained with the resolved path. Verified in-process and over a real pipe in the interop client. 604 tests pass.

title: Call the terminal/* client method family
description:
Consume create_terminal, terminal_output, wait_for_terminal_exit, kill_terminal, and release_terminal.

Terminals are stateful and leak: a created terminal must be released on every path including turn cancellation, session close (Phase 2.3), and client disconnect. Track live terminals per session so cleanup is possible.

output_byte_limit exists on CreateTerminalRequest for a reason -- unbounded output is a real failure mode. Set it.
acceptance_criteria: All five methods callable and gated on client capability; every created terminal is released on normal completion, cancellation, session close, and disconnect; live terminals tracked per session; output_byte_limit set to a documented default; tests cover the leak paths, not just the happy path.

Start every client call with context.require(Gate.X) from python_acp.turns -- READ_TEXT_FILE / WRITE_TEXT_FILE (two INDEPENDENT booleans under fs; a read grant must never satisfy a write), TERMINAL (one boolean for all five terminal/* methods, no per-method granularity exists), ELICITATION (advertised by presence of an empty marker model, so 'is not None', not bool(model)). UngatedClientCallError is a RuntimeError -> -32603 because an ungated call is our conformance bug. A client that declared nothing may be called for nothing. See src/python_acp/turns.md.
CORRECTION (2026-08-23), supersedes the "Start every client call with context.require(Gate.X)" line above. That guidance is hnk.1-era and predates pyacp-8bv.2, which established the split now in force:

  • context.allows(Gate.TERMINAL) at PARSE time -> a client that never advertised terminal gets TurnResult.refused(). This is the ordinary case and is NOT our bug.
  • context.require(Gate.TERMINAL) survives at the CALL SITE as an assertion of our own invariant -- parsing should already have refused, so reaching a client method ungated really is a conformance bug and -32603 is honest there.

Following the stale line literally reports -32603 for the ordinary "client does not do terminals" case, which lies to the client about whose fault it is. See src/python_acp/turn_mcp_router.py (_reads/_writes) and turns.md for the shape to copy. Still accurate from the original note: TERMINAL is ONE boolean for all five terminal/* methods -- no per-method granularity exists.

DISCONNECT, resolved (2026-08-23): the acceptance criterion "every created terminal is released on ... disconnect" cannot be met literally. Terminals live in the CLIENT; once it disconnects there is nobody to send terminal/release to. Sessions deliberately survive disconnect (sessions.py:368 -- a disconnecting client must not silently delete sessions another connection may use). Decision: on disconnect, DROP OUR TRACKING so we do not leak memory, and state plainly in the module doc that the terminals themselves are the departed clients to reap. Do not pretend to release them.

PATTERN, decided (2026-08-23): mirror src/python_acp/mcp_registry.py rather than inventing a second lifecycle shape. It already solves this: per-session tracking, close(session_id) wired to the SessionRegistry.on_close hook, close_all() for process shutdown with the explicit "not for a disconnect" distinction, and remove-the-entry-BEFORE-stopping ordering so a teardown that raises cannot leave a session addressable with dead resources.
close_reason: Merged to main. All five terminal/* methods callable and gated (allows-at-parse, require-at-call-site); per-session TerminalRegistry mirroring mcp_registry; released on completion, cancellation, and session close; disconnect drops tracking and releases nothing, as decided and documented. output_byte_limit defaults to 1 MiB, derived from the 8 MiB MCP stream limit. 664 tests pass; leak paths covered against real subprocesses.

title: Implement the extended lifecycle: load_session, resume_session, fork_session, list_sessions, close_session
description:
The optional-but-required-for-strict-full-v1 lifecycle surface. Depends on Phase 2.1's copy-versus-share decisions.

Each method implemented here must flip its corresponding literal in the initialize capability block (loadSession, sessionCapabilities.delete, and so on), per Phase 1.4's rule that advertisement matches reality.

Verify that before implementing. fork_session was absent from the original plan and must not alias the parent session's mutable state.

1. acp.contrib.session_state was evaluated and REPLACED for the registry (wrong direction:

title: Make the Makefile venv handling correct both in an activated venv and on a bare CI runner
description:
The Makefile assumes one environment shape and silently does the wrong thing in the other.

Local (this sandbox and any developer who has run 'source venv/bin/activate'): VIRTUAL_ENV=/Users/dave/dev/other/python-acp/venv and PATH starts with venv/bin, so the Makefile's 'PYTHON ?= python3' resolves to venv/bin/python3 -- the interpreter inside the venv make is about to manage. VENV_DIR resolves to 'venv' because that directory exists.

GitHub Actions (all four legs of the ci.yml matrix added in pyacp-0f6): a fresh checkout has neither .venv nor venv, so VENV_DIR falls through to '.venv', no venv is active, and 'python3' is whatever actions/setup-python put on PATH.

Concrete defects that follow:

1. 'make venv' never recreates an existing venv -- the recipe is guarded by 'if [ ! -d $(VENV_DIR) ]'. So 'make venv PYTHON=python3.12' on a machine that already has venv/ built from 3.14 does not build a 3.12 environment; it pip-installs into the 3.14 one and reports success. There is no supported way to reproduce a non-default matrix leg locally. Validating pyacp-0f6 required building .venv311/.venv312/.venv313 by hand, entirely outside the Makefile, precisely because of this.

2. VENV_DIR differs between the two environments ('venv' locally, '.venv' in CI) purely as a side effect of which directory happens to exist. Two developers on the same commit can be using different directories, and neither matches CI.

3. Every target depends on venv, and the venv recipe unconditionally runs 'pip install --upgrade pip' followed by 'pip install -e .[dev]'. So 'make test' always reaches the network. In a network-restricted sandbox that is a hard failure (pip cannot verify the proxy's TLS cert against Python's CA store, so make venv exits non-zero before any test runs); in CI it is wasted time on every invocation.

4. DEMO_MCP_COMMAND defaults to bare 'python3 tests/fixtures/mock_mcp_server.py' rather than $(PYTHON_BIN). 'make run' therefore launches the MCP subprocess on whatever python3 is on PATH while the bridge itself runs on $(VENV_DIR)/bin/python. Those coincide only when a venv is already activated -- exactly the local case, which is why it has never been noticed.
design:
Make the environment explicit instead of inferred.

- Pin VENV_DIR to a single default ('.venv') rather than deriving it from whichever directory exists, and keep it overridable. Decide what to do about the existing venv/ (support both for a transition, or document the rename).
- Make the venv recipe version-aware: record the interpreter used to build it (a stamp file, or read $(VENV_DIR)/bin/python --version) and rebuild when $(PYTHON) does not match, so 'make venv PYTHON=python3.12 VENV_DIR=.venv312' is the supported way to reproduce a matrix leg.
- Gate the pip install behind that stamp so lint/test/build stop hitting the network on every run; add an explicit 'make sync' or force flag for when deps genuinely changed.
- Point DEMO_MCP_COMMAND at $(PYTHON_BIN).
- If PYTHON resolves inside VENV_DIR itself (the activated-venv case), resolve it to the base interpreter or fail with a clear message rather than bootstrapping a venv from inside the venv it is replacing.

Verify by running the same make targets in both shapes: with venv activated, and in a container or fresh clone with no venv present.
acceptance_criteria: 'make venv PYTHON=<other-interpreter>' produces an environment on that interpreter even when a venv already exists, and every matrix leg from ci.yml is reproducible locally with a documented one-line command; 'make lint' and 'make test' succeed with no network access once the venv is provisioned; 'make run' launches the MCP subprocess on the venv interpreter; all four ci.yml legs stay green; CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md describe the venv contract, including which directory is canonical.

title: Reconcile Python version drift: local venv 3.14 vs CI 3.11
description: Local development runs Python 3.14.6 (repo venv/bin/python, based on /opt/homebrew/bin/python3) while both GitHub Actions workflows pin python-version: 3.11 (.github/workflows/ci.yml:18, .github/workflows/publish-artifacts.yml:17). pyproject.toml declares requires-python = '>=3.11', so 3.14 is nominally in range, but nothing in CI ever exercises it. Two minor versions of drift means local green does not imply CI green (and vice versa): 3.12-3.14 removed distutils, tightened asyncio deprecations, and changed several typing behaviors this codebase touches. Decide the supported range and make CI prove it.
design: Options: (a) add a CI matrix over 3.11 + 3.14 so both the floor and the local dev version are tested; (b) pin local dev to 3.11 to match CI exactly; (c) move CI to 3.14 and raise requires-python. Recommend (a): keep requires-python '>=3.11' honest by testing the declared floor and the newest supported release, and leave publish-artifacts.yml on the floor version for the widest-compatible wheel. Verify asyncio usage in mcp_stdio.py and ws_bridge.py against 3.14 deprecations while doing this.
