title: Decide whether /invokeTool and /tools still belong in the palette now that tools are announced natively
description:
`pyacp-acn` made every MCP tool callable by its own announced name — `/Demo/echo --text
"hi"` — which is how a client's composer now surfaces tools natively. That raises whether
the two built-ins that existed to reach tools the long way still earn their palette slots.

Raised by the user while verifying `pyacp-acn`: "we maybe should remove the /invokeTool
and even show tools since they now show up natively in the app. /Demo/echo will be the
normal way a tool is called."

**Recommendation: keep both commands; consider dropping only `/invokeTool` from the
announcement.**

`/invokeTool` is the escape hatch the sugar cannot cover:

- a tool whose name contains a slash. The sugar splits on the first slash and treats the
  rest as the tool, but `/invokeTool` takes a free-typed target;
- the bare form `/invokeTool echo --text x`, which omits the server. That is legal on a
  single-server session and the sugar has no equivalent, because a bare first token cannot
  be distinguished from prose without swallowing every non-JSON prompt.

Removing the *command* narrows what works. Removing only its *palette entry* stops
advertising a verb most users no longer need, while leaving it reachable — which is
probably the right shape.

`/tools` should stay in both. It prints every parameter with its type, required flag and
description; the native palette carries a name and one hint line. They answer different
questions, and `/tools` is what a listing footer points at.

Either removal changes advertised surface, so per the `acp-protocol` skill it wants its own
commit touching the manifests, `tests/test_conformance.py` if a disposition moves, the
co-located docs, and regenerated transcripts.

title: Reload the MCP catalogue without restarting the agent
description:
mcp_catalogue.load reads the file once, in cli._run, before a port is bound. There is no reload, and the module docstring says why: a catalogue that changed under a running process would leave open sessions advertising toggles for servers that no longer exist. Today an operator adding a server restarts the agent, which on the WebSocket transport drops every connected client and every live session.

That is the right FIRST behaviour -- correct and boring -- but it is a real operational cost for the deployment pyacp-lx7 was built for: a long-lived shared server is exactly the thing you do not want to restart to add a tool.

THE HARD PART IS NOT READING THE FILE, IT IS THE SESSIONS ALREADY OPEN. A session's config options are a deep copy taken at session/new, so after a reload a live session holds toggles that no longer match the catalogue. Four cases, each needing an answer:

1. ENTRY ADDED -- an open session has no option for it. Append one (and emit config_option_update, which exists for exactly this: 'an internally-originated change should look identical on the wire to a client-driven one'), or leave existing sessions alone and let only new ones see it?
2. ENTRY REMOVED while a session has it ON -- the server is running. Tear it down and drop the option, or keep it running until the session closes? Dropping an option a client is displaying needs config_option_update either way.
3. ENTRY CHANGED (different command/args) while running -- respawn, or leave the running one and let the change take effect on the next session? Respawning mid-session has the same broken-pipe problem as the toggle, which pyacp-lx7.3 answered by refusing during a turn.
4. THE NEW FILE IS INVALID -- must be a no-op that keeps the old catalogue and says so loudly, never a half-applied reload.

Whatever the answers, the palette follows: announce_commands (pyacp-p8v) is already the one door for that.

TRIGGER, also undecided: SIGHUP is the conventional one for a daemon and costs nothing; an ACP extension request would need a client to send it and this is an operator action, not a client one; watching the file with a poll or an OS watcher is the most convenient and the most surprising. SIGHUP is the likely answer, and is meaningless under --transport stdio, where the process is the client's child and restarting it is trivial.
acceptance_criteria:
1. A reload picks up added, removed, and changed entries.
2. Every one of the four open-session cases above has a decided, documented, tested answer -- this bead is not done by making the happy path work.
3. An invalid file leaves the running catalogue untouched and logs what was wrong.
4. Sessions whose options change get config_option_update, and the palette follows where tools changed.
5. Meaningless-under-stdio is handled explicitly rather than by accident.
6. mcp_catalogue.md's 'read once, at startup' paragraph is rewritten rather than left contradicting the code.
7. make lint && make docs-check && make test.

title: Expand URI templates client-side (RFC 6570) so /resourceShow can take arguments
description:
Once pyacp-as5 makes templates visible, the follow-on question is whether
`/resourceShow demo greeting --name ada` should work beside the concrete
`/resourceShow demo greeting://ada`.

DELIBERATELY DEFERRED, and the reason is the point: the concrete form already works and
needs nothing. Expansion buys ergonomics, not capability. So this is a P3 that should stay
open until someone actually asks, rather than being folded into the bug fix.

THE COST. MCP specifies RFC 6570, which is four levels of operators -- {var}, {+var},
{#var}, {.var}, {/var}, {;var}, {?var}, {&var}, plus explode modifiers {/list*} and
prefix modifiers {var:3}. A hand-rolled subset is silently wrong on whatever it skipped:
it produces a URI, just not the right one, and the server answers "unknown resource" for
a template the user read straight off the listing. So this is a real dependency decision
(PyPI `uritemplate` is the obvious candidate) and runtime dependencies here are
exact-pinned protocol surface, reviewed on their own -- see the Dependencies section of
CLAUDE.md. That review IS this bead, not a footnote to it.

THE DESIGN ASYMMETRY, which needs settling BEFORE it ships, not after. `/promptShow name
--arg v` works because the SERVER substitutes: prompts/get takes {name, arguments} and
hands back messages. Template expansion is the opposite -- the CLIENT substitutes and
resources/read only ever sees a finished URI. Two commands that look identical to a user
while running opposite mechanisms is exactly the kind of thing commands.md exists to
write down; the "Three primitives, and the one line that divides them" table currently
tells a reader that resources have no such split.

Consequence worth thinking through: a template argument that is wrong produces a
well-formed URI the server rejects, whereas a wrong prompt argument is caught by
/promptShow's own validation before the call. Decide whether this validates against the
template's variable list first (it can -- the variables are parseable from the template)
or lets the server refuse.
acceptance_criteria: A decision is recorded either way. If implemented: expansion is RFC 6570-correct (via a reviewed, exact-pinned dependency rather than a hand-rolled subset), /resourceShow accepts named arguments against a listed template, unknown variables are refused before the read, and commands.md documents that prompt expansion is server-side while resource expansion is client-side. If declined: commands.md says so and this closes as wontfix.

title: read_resource forwards an 'arguments' param MCP does not define
description:
`MCPStdioClient.read_resource(resource_id, arguments=None)` puts an `arguments` member on `resources/read` params when given one. MCP defines `resources/read` params as `{uri}` and nothing else. The mock fixture honours it, which is why no test has ever caught it; a real server ignores it.

The mcp-protocol skill has carried this as a known divergence. It matters more now: pyacp-tc5 gave `read_resource` its first ACP-facing caller (`/resourceShow`), and that caller deliberately does not pass `arguments` -- so the parameter is now dead weight that only the fixture and one test exercise.

WHAT TEMPLATED RESOURCES ACTUALLY NEED: a URI template like `greeting://{name}` is advertised by `resources/templates/list`, which this client does not wrap, and is expanded CLIENT-side into a concrete URI (RFC 6570) before `resources/read` is called. So the fix is two-sided if templates are wanted: drop the param, and optionally add `list_resource_templates()` on `_list_all` plus template expansion.

Dropping the param alone is small: the signature, the fixture's `arguments` handling, and `tests/test_mcp_stdio.py::test_list_prompts_get_prompt_and_read_resource_over_stdio`, which reads `greeting://{name}` with `{'name': 'Ava'}` today.
acceptance_criteria: read_resource takes a uri only; the fixture stops honouring a param real servers ignore; the mcp-protocol skill's known-divergence entry is removed or narrowed to the templates half.

title: A2A as a delegation layer above the bridge — tabled, research done
description:
**Tabled by the user on 2026-08-25.** Filed deferred so the research is recoverable and
the question is not re-litigated from scratch.

Research write-up (private artifact):
https://claude.ai/code/artifact/0aa7b0f7-8b55-493d-b777-2fe55d29c90e

## Conclusion

A2A is **not** an alternative to ACP -- it is the layer above it, and the two are designed
to stack. A2A's own docs put it plainly: an application uses A2A to talk to other agents,
while each agent internally uses MCP for its tools. This bridge already occupies the MCP
half of that sentence. Swapping ACP for A2A loses a capability rather than gaining one.

The blocking fact is not technical: **there is no peer to delegate to yet.** A2A's entire
value is cross-boundary delegation, so building the server before a peer exists pays the
dependency and deployment cost for a capability nothing calls.

## Do not re-derive these

- A2A is v1.0 (2026, Linux Foundation, 150+ orgs). `a2a-sdk` 1.1.2, `requires-python >=3.10`.
- The 0.3 -> 1.0 migration broke nearly every wire surface: `message/send` -> `SendMessage`,
  lowercase enums -> `TASK_STATE_SUBMITTED` / `ROLE_USER`, Text/File/DataPart unified into
  one `Part` discriminated by member, `mimeType` -> `mediaType`, cursor pagination,
  `supportedInterfaces[]` on the AgentCard. Most tutorials in circulation are pre-1.0.
- Concepts map cleanly: MCP tool -> AgentSkill; ACP session -> contextId; turn -> Task;
  `session/update` -> TaskStatusUpdateEvent; `stopReason` -> terminal TaskState.
- Cost: `a2a-sdk` pulls protobuf, google-api-core, googleapis-common-protos, httpx,
  json-rpc, plus Starlette/FastAPI to serve and SQLAlchemy to persist Tasks. **Never
  measured** -- see acceptance criteria.
- Worth stealing regardless: each A2A `AgentInterface` declares its own `protocolVersion`,
  so one agent serves several versions at once. Same problem the ACP v2 draft poses
  (pyacp-u2y), and `SUPPORTED_PROTOCOL_VERSIONS` is already a set for exactly this reason.

## The two hard questions, unanswered

1. **What is a Task?** One turn means inheriting turn semantics and gaining little. A Task
   that outlives its connection needs storage and a lifecycle this bridge has never had.
2. **Who answers the permission prompt?** `session/request_permission` assumes a human is
   present; `TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED` puts them across a network or removes them.
   `mcp_tools.py` refuses to let a server's own `readOnlyHint` skip the prompt, so
   weakening it for a remote caller would undo that reasoning.
acceptance_criteria:
Reopen only when a concrete peer agent exists to delegate to. Then, in order:

- Measure first: install a2a-sdk into a throwaway venv and record the site-packages and
  container-image deltas the way pyacp-8ub did for pydantic. Reasoned estimates do not
  meet this repo's bar.
- Generate an AgentCard from a live session by mapping tools/list to AgentSkill entries,
  and judge whether it reads as honest. If MCP tool schemas do not make convincing skills,
  the layering is weaker than it looks on paper. Costs nothing and serves nothing.
- Only then decide the Task lifetime and the permission question above.
- If it ships: a separate transport beside transport_ws.py and transport_stdio.py, behind
  its own optional extra. The ACP surface must not learn that A2A exists.

title: STATISTICS.md: a generated codebase-statistics doc, maintained by make stats
description:
Requested: a STATISTICS.md at the repo root recording lines, modules, classes, functions, and tests, kept up to date under the repo-docs-sync rules.

Hand-written numbers are wrong the day after they are written, so the doc is GENERATED: scripts/code_stats.py counts via the AST (a def inside a docstring is not a function) and 'make stats' rewrites the file. The doc stamps the commit it was generated from so a reader can see how stale it is.

What IS checked is the invariant that can silently rot: STATISTICS.md must list every production module and no others -- the same class of rule check_docs.py already enforces for co-located docs.
design: scripts/code_stats.py holds the counting; 'make stats' regenerates; --check reports staleness without writing, so a future CI gate needs no new code. tests/test_code_stats.py tests the counter against a fixture with known contents rather than against the repo, so the test does not move every time the repo does.

title: Real authentication for the WebSocket transport, beyond a shared key
description:
pyacp-rg8 adds a shared access key checked before the WebSocket handshake. That closes 'wide open' but it is deliberately the cheapest thing that works, and it has known limits worth naming before someone assumes otherwise:

  * ONE key for every client. No identity, so no per-client revocation and nothing to attribute a session to. The agent cannot tell two clients apart, which also means session/list shows every client every session.
  * NO TLS anywhere in this process. The key travels in the request URL, so it is readable by anything on the path and lands in proxy and server access logs, which are exactly the places URLs get written down.
  * A query parameter is the wrong carrier on principle -- Authorization or a Sec-WebSocket-Protocol token keeps it out of the URL -- and was chosen because it is the one thing every WebSocket client library can send without custom header support.
  * Rotation means a restart.

Open questions for whoever picks this up, none of them settled here: whether ACP's own authenticate/AUTH_METHODS is the right home (the acp-protocol skill notes the empty authMethods list is bound by test to the absence of a remote MCP transport, so reopening one reopens the other); whether to terminate TLS here or require a reverse proxy and say so; whether per-client identity is worth the session-model change it forces.

Not blocking anything. Filed so the shared key is understood as a floor rather than the answer.
design: Deliberately unscoped. Decide the threat model first -- who is the attacker and where does the socket live -- because 'a trusted LAN behind a tunnel' and 'the open internet' want different answers and only the second justifies the session-model change.

title: Flip the default --transport to stdio now that ws carries nothing extra
description:
--transport defaults to ws. That default was chosen when the WebSocket surface carried something stdio did not: the deprecated {action:...} API and the MCP passthrough. pyacp-sld.3 deleted both, so the two transports now serve the identical agent -- same initialize negotiation, same capability block, same error codes, same methods.

The argument for flipping: stdio is how an editor spawns an ACP agent (decision D2), it is the shape the SDK's own examples assume, and it needs no port. A first-time user running 'python -m python_acp.cli' with no arguments currently gets a listening socket rather than an agent on their pipes.

The argument against, which is why this is filed rather than done: it breaks every existing invocation that relies on the default, for no capability gain. That is a release-note-worthy change and belongs to whoever cuts the release, not to a refactor.

cli.md currently records that the flip was expected 'when the action surface is removed' and that it has not happened, with the reason.
acceptance_criteria: Either --transport defaults to stdio, with the change noted wherever the default is documented (cli.md, README, Makefile run target), or the decision to keep ws as the default is recorded in cli.md with its reasoning and this issue closes.
close_reason: Decided: ws stays the default. Recorded in cli.md as a dated decision with the real reason -- v0.1.0 and v0.1.1 shipped WebSocket-only (CLI was --mcp-command/--host/--port, no --transport flag), so every released invocation binds a socket, and since pyacp-sld.3 the two transports serve an identical agent, so the flip buys no capability. README and test_ws_stays_the_default_transport carry the same reasoning. Revisit only alongside a release already breaking the CLI contract.

title: A forwarded elicitation carries no toolCallId, so a client cannot attach the question to the tool call that provoked it
description:
ElicitationFormSessionMode takes an optional toolCallId, and elicitation.py leaves it unset.

A client rendering the form therefore shows it detached from the tool call it belongs to -- which is exactly the case the field exists for: an MCP server asks for input in the middle of a tools/call, and the UI should attach the question to that call's entry rather than float it beside the transcript.

The id is known where it is needed and not where it is used. turn_mcp_router._run emits the ToolCallStart and holds the id; the elicitation handler runs on MCPStdioClient's read-loop dispatch, in a task of its own, with no link back to the caller. contextvars do not cross that boundary, because the task is created from the read loop rather than from the caller.

Options to weigh:

1. Track the in-flight tool call per (backend, request id). mcp_stdio knows which of OUR requests are outstanding; an elicitation arriving while exactly one tools/call is in flight on that backend is almost certainly about it. 'Almost certainly' is the weakness -- concurrent calls on one backend make it a guess, and a wrong toolCallId is worse than none.
2. Have the router register the current tool call id on the session before calling, and have the forwarder read it. Correct only while a session runs one turn at a time, which sessions.py does enforce (TurnAlreadyRunningError) -- but a turn may run several invocations, and only sequentially today.
3. Leave it unset. Honest, and what ships now.

Option 2 looks strongest given the one-turn-at-a-time rule, but it puts turn state somewhere the read loop can see it, which is a real coupling to design rather than to bolt on.
acceptance_criteria: Either a forwarded elicitation carries the toolCallId of the invocation that provoked it, with a test proving it is the right one and not merely present, or the decision to leave it unset is recorded in elicitation.md with the reasoning that settles it.
notes: discovered-from: pyacp-8bv.4
close_reason:
Option 2 from the bead, taken because the constraint it depends on is real and enforced rather than incidental: sessions.py's attach_turn refuses a second concurrent turn, and a turn runs its invocations in order, so at most one MCP call is ever in flight per session. That makes 'the tool call this session is inside' unique rather than a guess.

turn_mcp_router parks the tracker's real toolCallId on Session.running_tool_call for exactly the length of client.call_tool, cleared in finally so a call that raised cannot leave a stale id for the next question. elicitation.forwarder takes a RunningToolCall lookup -- a callable, not a value, because the id changes constantly and one captured at session/new would name a call that finished long ago -- and agent._running_tool_call reads it by session id, answering None for an unknown session (session/close racing an elicitation already in flight).

Option 1 (guess from in-flight requests in mcp_stdio) was rejected as the bead expected: concurrent calls on one backend make it a guess, and a wrong toolCallId is worse than none.

Proved end to end, not just plumbed: the fixture's provoke tool sends elicitation/create and blocks until answered, so the question really is in flight INSIDE tools/call, and the test asserts the id the forwarded question carried equals the toolCallId the turn actually streamed -- plus that it is cleared afterwards. Two unit tests cover the callable-not-value property and that None (a server eliciting outside any tools/call) is ordinary rather than a fallback.

The dependency on one-turn-at-a-time is recorded in three places -- the field's docstring, sessions.md, elicitation.md -- and in the mcp-protocol skill, because relaxing it would need a different mechanism rather than a patch to this one. Golden transcripts unchanged.

title: A malformed mcpServers entry is silently dropped, so session/new can hand back a session whose tools do not exist
description:
The SDK parses session/new's mcpServers with skip_invalid_items, so an entry that does not match McpServerStdio (a typo'd key, a missing command) is removed from the list BEFORE PythonAcpAgent.new_session is called. The agent then opens the servers that survived, succeeds, and returns a sessionId. The client asked for N servers and got a session backed by fewer, with no error and no warning.

That is precisely the failure mcp_registry's all-or-nothing opening exists to prevent -- 'a partially-opened session would hand back an id whose tools silently do not exist' -- arriving by a route mcp_registry cannot see, because by then the entry is gone.

Made visible by pyacp-6ni.3: tests/test_negative.py::test_a_malformed_mcp_server_entry_is_dropped_not_refused pins it as current behaviour so an SDK change is noticed, but pinning is not fixing.

Options, none of them free:
1. Compare counts at the transport. transport_ws.py still has the raw dict before the SDK decodes it; it could count params.mcpServers and hand the agent the raw length, or refuse when the parsed list is shorter. Costs a layering violation -- the transport would need to know which method carries which list -- and does nothing for stdio unless duplicated there.
2. Ask the SDK to stop salvaging. Whether skip_invalid_items is configurable per call site is unknown; agent-client-protocol is pre-1.0 and this may be worth an upstream issue.
3. Accept it and document it in the README, on the grounds that a client sending a malformed server spec has a bug of its own. Weakest option: the whole point of the all-or-nothing rule is that silent partial success is worse than loud failure.

Related SDK-salvage behaviour: a junk protocolVersion becomes the default rather than -32602 (also pinned in test_negative.py). That one is benign by comparison -- the client learns the negotiated version in the reply.
acceptance_criteria: Either session/new refuses a request whose mcpServers contained an unparseable entry, or the decision to accept it is recorded with its reasoning in agent.md and the README; the pinning test is updated to match whichever holds.
notes: Do not 'fix' this by removing the pinning test. The test is what makes the behaviour visible; if the decision is to accept the salvage, the test stays and its docstring records why.
close_reason:
Closed with the decision recorded: the drop is ACCEPTED, and the reasoning is the protocol's, not convenience.

The bead listed three options and judged 'accept and document' the weakest. That judgement was made without the decisive fact: skip_invalid_items restores the ACP schema's own x-deserialize-skip-invalid-items annotation, and the schema carries it on 35 FIELDS -- mcpServers on all four session methods, plus additionalDirectories, availableModes, configOptions, content, locations, authMethods and more -- beside 84 fields marked x-deserialize-default-on-error. That is a deliberate protocol-wide posture: drop what you cannot parse rather than failing the message. Refusing here would not close a gap; it would be one agent opting out of ACP's robustness rule on one field, and doing it consistently would mean opting out on all 35.

Option 1 (compare counts at the transport) is also unavailable in practice, and for a stronger reason than the bead gave: acp.router validates inside its own wrapper, so NO ACP method can see raw params, and the only place holding the original dict is transport_ws.receive(). transport_stdio has no equivalent seam -- the SDK owns that read loop -- so the fix would work on WebSocket and not stdio. Behaviour that depends on how a client connected is worse than a documented limitation.

DELIVERED, because 'accept' should not mean 'do nothing'. The one place a client feels this is naming an absent server in a prompt, where 'this session opened [x]' reads like their own typo. That refusal now names the dropped-entry possibility and the four required fields. Also found: all four of name/command/args/env are required with no defaults, so a plausible entry like {name, command} is dropped exactly like nonsense -- pinned by a new test using that realistic shape.

Recorded in agent.md (with why refusing was rejected and where it could not be done) and README (a call-out telling clients to send all four fields, args and env as [] when empty). Pinning tests kept and their docstrings now carry the decision, so an SDK bump that stops salvaging re-opens it deliberately.

title: A turn cancelled during terminal/create leaks a terminal we never learned the id of
description: If a turn is cancelled after the client has started the process but before the terminal/create response arrives, we never learn the terminal id, so it cannot be released or tracked. This is the ordinary lost-reply problem and no code on our side can close it; documented in terminals.md under 'The window this does not close'. Filed so it is tracked rather than only narrated. Possible mitigations to evaluate: shield the create call itself, or reconcile against a client-side terminal list if ACP ever offers one.
notes: discovered-from: pyacp-8bv.3
close_reason:
Closed by FIXING it, not by documenting it. The bead and terminals.md both said no code on our side could close this window -- 'the id existed only in a response that was never delivered'. That was too strong, and the bead's own first mitigation was the answer: the reply WAS delivered, to a future nobody was waiting on any more because our own cancellation dropped it.

TerminalRegistry.create now runs the create_terminal request as a task and awaits it under asyncio.shield, so our cancellation does not take the request with it. On CancelledError, _abandon_unclaimed waits (bounded, _UNCLAIMED_CREATE_TIMEOUT = 5s) for the id, tracks the terminal, and abandons it -- kill + release, the same call _capture makes for a command cancelled a moment later, for the same reason: nobody is left to read the output. Under shield again, because the cancellation is already in flight. CancelledError is re-raised.

Tracked before abandoned even though released a line later, because session/close can be running concurrently and a terminal the registry cannot see is one close cannot clean up.

Residual window, now much narrower and documented as such: a reply that never arrives AT ALL, which is the connection dying underneath us. Bounded so the cancellation cannot hang, and logged with the command name.

The regression test was verified to FAIL without the shield -- released == [] and the leak warning fires -- rather than assumed to be meaningful. Three tests: reply lands late and is released, reply never lands and does not hang, and the ordinary create the shield must not disturb.

The bead's second mitigation (reconcile against a client-side terminal list) stays unavailable: acp.interfaces.Client has create/output/wait_for_exit/kill/release and no list method.

terminals.md's 'The window this does not close' section rewritten to say what was wrong with it; compliance matrix's terminal note updated; the leak-path test table gained all three rows. Golden transcripts unchanged.

title: A turn outlives the session/prompt request that died
description:
agent.prompt's 'except asyncio.CancelledError' branch cancels the turn task and re-raises without awaiting it, so between the request dying and the task's next await the executor can still emit session/update notifications for a request nobody is reading. Not the same hole as pyacp-hnk.5's 'nothing emits after the response' guarantee, which is structural: on the normal path the response is built only after asyncio.wait({turn}) returns, so nothing can follow it. This is the no-response path.

Deliberately left alone in pyacp-hnk.5: awaiting the turn inside a cancelled request is how you turn a dead request into a hang if an executor ignores cancellation, and no shipped executor emits after being cancelled. Options if it ever matters: await the task under a short asyncio.wait_for so the window is bounded, or have TurnContext refuse to emit once its turn is detached. The second is enforcement rather than a convention, but it makes a late emit raise inside a detached task.

Reproduce: an executor that emits from an 'except CancelledError' handler under asyncio.shield, with the session/prompt request itself cancelled (not session/cancel).
close_reason: TurnContext.detach() in prompt's finally; emit raises DetachedTurnError afterwards. Chose the bead's second option (enforcement) over the bounded wait_for, since shield defeats any convention. session/cancel path unaffected and guarded by a test. Verified by removing the fix: 3 of 4 new tests fail.

title: MCP tool annotations would let permission distinguish reads from deletes
description: turn_mcp_router asks the client for permission before EVERY tool call, because MCP 2024-11-05 has no tool annotations and there is no way to tell a read from a delete. readOnlyHint / destructiveHint / idempotentHint / openWorldHint arrive in MCP 2025-03-26. If _SUPPORTED_MCP_PROTOCOL_VERSIONS ever widens to include a revision that has them, the router can skip the prompt for readOnlyHint tools and mark destructiveHint ones more prominently. Blocked on the protocol-version bump, not on a heuristic -- see .claude/skills/mcp-protocol/spec-versions.md before widening the pin.
close_reason: Unblocked and done: the bead said 'blocked on the protocol-version bump', but pyacp-pb7 already moved the pin to 2025-06-18 for elicitation and annotations arrived in 2025-03-26. New mcp_tools.py maps readOnlyHint/destructiveHint/openWorldHint onto ACP ToolCall.kind, with a per-turn tools/list cache (lazy per server, best-effort for kinds, strict for available_commands). REFUSED the bead's suggestion to skip the prompt for readOnlyHint tools: a server asserting read-only to escape the permission prompt is a privilege escalation written by the party being restrained, and MCP's own spec says never to make tool-use decisions on annotations. A hint relabels the question; it never withdraws it. Two mapping decisions recorded: unstated hints stay 'other' EXCEPT destructiveHint, where MCP's true default means 'assume the worst' and feeds a warning; and destructive rounds to 'delete' rather than 'edit' because understating risk in a permission prompt is the worse error. Behaviour change: announce-tools no longer avoids every tools/list -- a turn still lists the servers it calls. Option description and its test docstring corrected; three golden transcripts re-recorded (diff read: kind other->read on the tool_call AND on the permission request, which is still sent).

title: Carry the legacy MCP passthrough methods on ext_method during the transition
description:
The JSON-RPC surface today includes direct MCP passthrough -- tools/list, tools/call, prompts/list, prompts/get, resources/list, resources/read -- which are MCP method names, not ACP ones. They do not belong in an ACP agent's method table once dispatch comes from acp.agent.router.

The SDK's Agent protocol has ext_method and ext_notification precisely as the escape hatch for non-spec methods. Move the passthrough there under a namespaced prefix, so it stays available through the migration without polluting the ACP surface.

Decide whether passthrough survives removal at all, or whether tool access should go exclusively through session/prompt once the tool-router executor exists.
acceptance_criteria: MCP passthrough reachable via ext_method under a documented namespace; no MCP method names remain in the ACP method table; existing consumers have a documented migration path; the long-term fate of passthrough is decided and recorded.
close_reason:
Closed as DECLINED, with the decision recorded rather than the move made. The bead asked for two things: move the MCP passthrough onto ext_method under a namespace, and decide whether passthrough survives at all. The second answer settles the first -- it does not survive, so the move is churn that would cost clients two breaking changes instead of one.

Three reasons: (1) the passthrough addresses the process-wide --mcp-command server, the exact arrangement ACP v1 inverted, so a namespaced _tools/call would preserve the pre-v1 architecture behind a new name and keep --mcp-command alive to serve it; (2) two breaking changes for a surface being deleted either way; (3) the bead's stated motive -- 'MCP method names do not belong in the ACP method table' -- is already satisfied, because transport_ws.receive() intercepts them before the SDK sees them and they were never in the router's table.

Confirmed with the user: passthrough dies with the legacy surface; no known consumers.

DELIVERED, because the old plan had put a false promise on the wire: ACTION_REPLACEMENTS named JSON-RPC targets (list_tools -> tools/list) that now die in the same release, so it was telling clients to migrate to something that disappears with them. It now names the ACP path (session/new + session/prompt) for the two actions that have one, and None for the five that do not -- MCP prompts, resources, and ping have no ACP counterpart. deprecation_notice omits 'use' for those; warn_deprecated gained a third branch so an operator is told the capability goes away, not just the spelling. README migration table rewritten to say what is lost. Recorded in legacy_ws.py/.md, agent.py/.md, docs/acp-compliance-matrix.md, docs/module-boundaries.md, docs/full-apc-plan.md 7.2, and pyacp-sld.3's notes.

title: Abstract the backend so non-MCP executors are possible
description:
Original plan item 6.3. Largely satisfied by Phase 3.1's TurnExecutor interface -- the point of that seam is that MCP stops being the only thing a turn can drive.

This issue is the remainder: make sure nothing MCP-specific leaks through the session registry, the capability advertisement, or the update-emission path, so that a second backend could be added without touching them. Verify by writing a trivial non-MCP executor as a test double rather than by inspection.

Reassess after Phase 3.1 lands -- this may close as already-done.

close_reason: Closed as already-achieved, with the finding proved rather than asserted. The TurnExecutor seam from Phase 3.1 IS the backend abstraction; no second one was added. tests/test_executor_neutrality.py: a complete non-MCP executor (declares all three descriptive attributes, emits real session/updates, reads its own mode) serves create -> set_mode -> prompt -> close through the SDK router; an AST walk holds sessions.py, capabilities.py and turns.py free of any backend import; build_agent_capabilities' signature is pinned so the block cannot learn about a backend. title: Drive elicitation/create and elicitation/complete
description:
Consume the client's elicitation flow so the runtime can ask the user a structured question mid-turn.

This is also the ACP side of pyacp-pb7: an MCP server can send elicitation/create to us as its client, and the natural implementation is to forward it to the ACP client's elicitation flow. That forwarding is the strongest argument for declaring the elicitation capability in the MCP initialize request, and it requires bumping the pinned MCP protocol version to 2025-06-18. Sequence this issue with pyacp-pb7 deliberately.

Note create_elicitation is a request and complete_elicitation is a notification -- different shapes.
acceptance_criteria: Both elicitation methods driven correctly, gated on client capability; an MCP-server-initiated elicitation/create can be forwarded to the ACP client and its answer returned to the MCP server; the relationship to pyacp-pb7 is resolved rather than duplicated; tests cover forwarding and the no-capability path.
notes: pyacp-hnk.1: gating lives on the turn seam, not at each call site. Start every client call with context.require(Gate.X) from python_acp.turns -- READ_TEXT_FILE / WRITE_TEXT_FILE (two INDEPENDENT booleans under fs; a read grant must never satisfy a write), TERMINAL (one boolean for all five terminal/* methods, no per-method granularity exists), ELICITATION (advertised by presence of an empty marker model, so 'is not None', not bool(model)). UngatedClientCallError is a RuntimeError -> -32603 because an ungated call is our conformance bug. A client that declared nothing may be called for nothing. See src/python_acp/turns.md.
close_reason: Elicitation forwarding lands: elicitation.py turns an MCP server's elicitation/create into an ACP form-mode, session-scoped one and hands the answer back. complete_elicitation declined structurally (elicitationId exists only on the URL variants, and nothing here creates one). Gate.ELICITATION split into ELICITATION_FORM/ELICITATION_URL -- ElicitationCapabilities is a container, not the marker the docs claimed. title: Cover the real WebSocket opening handshake without bind()
description: tests/test_mcp_stdio.py::test_websocket_bridge_lists_and_calls_tools_prompts_and_resources and ::test_websocket_bridge_handles_jsonrpc_initialize both call _free_port(), which does socket.bind(('127.0.0.1', 0)). Sandboxed environments (including the one pyacp-0f6 was validated in) deny bind() for AF_INET and AF_UNIX alike, so those two tests fail with PermissionError before exercising any project code. That is 2 of 20 tests -- and specifically the only two that cover the real opening handshake and framing -- silently unavailable wherever an agent or CI runner is network-restricted.
design: Both tests can run without binding anything: pair socket.socketpair() with loop.connect_accepted_socket() for the server side and websockets.connect(uri, sock=...) for the client side. The server needs a WebSocketServer whose wrap() target stubs .sockets, .get_loop(), and .is_serving(). A working proof of this ran all of both tests' assertions unchanged on 3.11/3.12/3.13/3.14 during pyacp-0f6. Options: (a) replace _free_port() with a socketpair fixture outright, (b) keep the TCP path and add a socketpair fallback when bind() raises PermissionError. Prefer (a) -- one transport path, no environment-dependent branching, and nothing about these tests actually needs a TCP port.
acceptance_criteria: Both tests pass in an environment where socket.bind() raises PermissionError; they still assert the same responses they do today; make lint && make test green on every version in the ci.yml matrix; if the harness moves to a shared fixture, tests/ gains no dependency the dev extra does not already provide.
notes:
pyacp-tzd.3 removed the PermissionError half of this bead. The two tests it names no
longer exist: tests/test_transport_ws.py replaced them with socket-free equivalents that
drive a FakeWebSocket through serve_websocket(), and the whole suite (178 tests) now
passes in a sandbox that denies bind().

What is LEFT is the coverage gap this bead's DESIGN already solves. Nothing now exercises
websockets.asyncio.server.serve(), the real opening handshake, or real frame
transmission -- FakeWebSocket bypasses all three. Untested surface is
WebSocketAgentServer.start()/stop()/serve_forever(); _handle_client is covered by
test_the_server_binds_each_accepted_socket_to_an_agent.

The DESIGN's option (a) still applies verbatim: socket.socketpair() +
loop.connect_accepted_socket() for the server, websockets.connect(uri, sock=...) for the
client, needing a stub with .sockets/.get_loop()/.is_serving(). Note the server API moved
from websockets.serve to websockets.asyncio.server.serve, so the wrap() target is now a
ServerConnection rather than a WebSocketServerProtocol.
close_reason: Real serve()/handshake/frames covered over socketpair + connect_accepted_socket, no bind(); start/stop/serve_forever and the 50MiB max_size now exercised. Verified on 3.11 and 3.14 (745 each). Matrix run also caught and fixed environment-path leakage in the pyacp-6ni.2 golden transcripts.

title: Plan the websockets 12.0 -> 15.x upgrade off the deprecated legacy asyncio API
description: pyproject.toml pins websockets==12.0 (released Oct 2023). ws_bridge.py imports websockets.serve and websockets.server.WebSocketServerProtocol, both part of the legacy asyncio implementation that websockets 13 deprecates and 14+ moves behind websockets.legacy with a DeprecationWarning; the modern surface is websockets.asyncio.server.serve and ServerConnection. Confirmed during pyacp-0f6 that 12.0 imports clean with no warnings on 3.11-3.14, so this is not urgent -- but the pin is what makes newer interpreters safe, and it cannot be bumped without touching the bridge. Note websockets 12.0 installs the pure-Python py3-none-any wheel on 3.13/3.14 since its cp-specific wheels stop at cp312.
design: Migrate ws_bridge.py to websockets.asyncio.server: serve() returns an asyncio Server, the handler receives a ServerConnection instead of WebSocketServerProtocol, and the async-iteration and send() surface the bridge uses is unchanged. title: PytestUnraisableExceptionWarning from a subprocess transport on Python 3.11 only
description:
Running the suite on 3.11 emits one warning that 3.14 does not:

  tests/test_transport_stdio.py::test_a_session_can_bring_its_own_mcp_server
  PytestUnraisableExceptionWarning: Exception ignored in:
  <function BaseSubprocessTransport.__del__>
  ... asyncio/base_subprocess.py line 126, in __del__ -> self.close()

The suite passes; this is cleanup noise from an asyncio subprocess transport being
garbage-collected after its loop is gone. It is version-specific (3.11 present, 3.14
absent), so it is most likely a CPython asyncio change rather than anything this repo
does wrong -- but the test does spawn an MCP server subprocess for a session and may
not be tearing it down before the loop closes.

Found while running the ci.yml matrix locally for pyacp-22w. Not caused by that work:
it reproduces on 3.11 with or without those changes.

Worth either fixing the teardown so the transport is closed explicitly, or -- if it is
genuinely a CPython artefact -- adding a targeted filterwarnings with a comment naming
the version, so a NEW unraisable exception is not hidden by a blanket ignore.
acceptance_criteria: Either the 3.11 leg is warning-free, or the warning is suppressed by a narrowly-scoped filter that names the interpreter version and the reason, and a new unraisable exception in another test would still surface.
notes:
Confirmed in GitHub Actions on the 3.11 leg (CPython 3.11.16, ubuntu runner), not just locally — so it is not a macOS or a local-venv artefact.

Note it is NOT a single test. Locally it surfaced on
  tests/test_transport_stdio.py::test_a_session_can_bring_its_own_mcp_server
and in CI on
  tests/test_terminals.py::test_close_all_releases_every_session
Same traceback both times: BaseSubprocessTransport.__del__ -> close() -> call_soon() ->
RuntimeError('Event loop is closed'). It attaches to whichever test happens to be running
when the GC collects a subprocess transport whose loop has already closed, which means a
filterwarnings scoped to one test id would be wrong AND fragile.

That points at the real cause: some test spawns an asyncio subprocess and lets the
transport outlive its event loop instead of closing it. Fixing the teardown is preferable
to suppressing; the suppression fallback should be a global filter naming 3.11 and this
RuntimeError text specifically, so an unrelated unraisable exception still surfaces.

Only 3.11 and 3.14 checked locally (3.12/3.13 not installed on the dev machine); the CI
matrix covers all four and only 3.11 warns.
close_reason:
Reproduced on a real 3.11.15 venv and fixed. It was NOT a CPython artefact -- it was four separate subprocess leaks in this suite, and the warning was a bad detector for all of them.

Found by wrapping asyncio.create_subprocess_exec in a conftest, holding a STRONG reference to every process (a weakref hides exactly the case that warns -- my first probe reported '0 unclosed' while the warning was still firing), and checking _transport._closed at session finish.

Four causes, three of them the same mistake:
1. tests/test_conformance.py::make_router built SessionRegistry() with no on_close=backends.close. That hook is the entire coupling between sessions and their MCP subprocesses (decision B6a), so session/close closed sessions while their servers kept running.
2. wire() in test_negative.py, recording_socket() in test_transcripts.py, and bound_socket() in test_transport_ws.py all hung up without closing their sessions. A disconnect deliberately does not close sessions, so sessions.close_all() -- what cli.py does on the way out -- is what a harness has to do too. Three independent harnesses forgot the same wiring.
3. TerminalClient.release_terminal raised its simulated release_error BEFORE reaping, and the Awkward subclass in test_one_failing_release_does_not_strand_the_rest overrode release entirely without reaping. Both now reap first: release_error models a client answering -32603, not one walking away from its own subprocess.
4. My own SlowCreateClient from pyacp-9hd, whose create_terminal is cancelled after the process is already running -- it now reaps on CancelledError.

The bead offered 'fix the teardown' or 'add a targeted filterwarnings'. Neither alone is enough and the second is close to useless: the warning is GC-timing dependent (verified -- with a leak deliberately reintroduced, an error-level filterwarnings run still passed), it names whichever test was executing rather than the one that leaked, and 3.14 never emits it at all. So both, plus a real guard: tests/conftest.py fails the run deterministically, names the creating test, and was verified to catch a reintroduced leak on BOTH 3.11 and 3.14 and to pass clean on both.

filterwarnings = error::pytest.PytestUnraisableExceptionWarning is kept as a second net for unraisables from other sources. Note the guard's strong references stop the warning firing at all, so the guard replaces it as the detector -- removing tests/conftest.py brings the leaks back silently, and it says so.

834 tests pass on 3.11.15 and 3.14.6; transcripts unchanged.
